During the question period I made a suggestion to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) which, I was pleased to see, he did not categorically reject. He said that he did not think the steps I suggested, and upon which I will elaborate now, need be categorically rejected in terms of being useful at any time, but he said they would not be useful now. I should like to make the following proposal to the Postmaster General, with the additional emphasis that it be done now and that we do not wait any longer.
I would like to ask the Postmaster General to get in touch as soon as possible with the postal workers to agree mutually upon a single mediator who could be called in now. Clearly we need such a person because, both in terms of the issues at stake and in terms of a certain personality conflict, I think-

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext:
Just a minute. I think we need someone who could deal with the issues and bring the conflicting personalities together. Second, this mediator would have the task of bringing the two sides together to try immediately to get a mutually agreeable series of propositions. Third, after 72 hours, if there has not been an agreement reached by the two sides, the mediator would publish his set of recommendations. Fourth, these published recommendations, after the 72 hour period if no agreement is reached, would be considered by the government and by the trade union negotiators. If no agreement is reached by a mediator, these proposals would then be submitted to the membership of the union for their consideration together with their trade union negotiating team's recommendation as to whether the membership should or should not accept the mediator's proposal.
It seems to me that that would be a constructive move at this time because it would not force acceptance upon the trade union membership of a set of proposals that their democratically elected membership has rejected. For me it has a very important element of fairness in it in that it recognizes-and I want to say something very briefly about the details of the points that are still in dispute-the possibility during the next 72 hours of getting a mutually agreeable solution, and that of course would be the best one by far because there are quite a number of clauses that are not in agreement yet.
The minister knows that once you get rid of the trivial matters there are, relatively speaking, a handful of issues at stake and I submit that concerning the handful of major issues at stake the positions of both sides are not radically different, that the two sides are not far apart on the important questions. Therefore, I suggest that the mediator could play a constructive role in trying to bring these people together.
What are a few of the basic issues that seem to be worthy of consideration, and worthy of some move both on the part of the Post Office and on the part of the union? First of all, there is the union's concern for a reduction in the work week. What the union wants is not something that is new; it is something that is possessed by many workers, in Canada, and indeed it is possessed in principle by over 60 per cent of the federal public employees. What they want is to reduce the work week from 40 to 35 hours. The govern-
November 17, 1975

ment will not budge, but I repeat that over 60 per cent of public employees in Canada now have 37 'A hours. That at least is a position somewhere between what the government is offering now to the postal workers and what the union itself wants. It is surely something in which a mediator could play a useful role.
Second, the trade union is concerned that the mail handlers' salaries be improved. I ask you, Madam Speaker, and I appeal to members of parliament to consider the point they are making here. There are approximately 2,500 mail handlers as compared to some 18,500 postal clerks. At present the mail handlers-that very small minority of the total-get some 36 cents an hour less than the postal clerks.
What the postal workers want is to remove that disparity between the two sets of workers involved in essentially the same activity, and it seems to me that that is a very reasonable request. They want for that very small group of 2,500 workers, to remove that 36 cent an hour differential which exists between them and the 18,500 postal clerks. I say that in terms of equity and fairness it seems a reasonable proposition, and that in terms of the cost to the Treasury it is infinitesimally small. So again I say that there is surely a role for a mediator to play. In terms of what the union wants it seems to me that a good case could be made for going all the way, but at least we could move some way in that direction.
Third, there is the COLA clause. The government, as hon. members may know-I am sure the Conservatives have looked at all the details with great care and consideration as they usually do in such matters-in terms of its COLA clause proposals will give 1 cent an hour for every 4 per cent increase in the consumer price index up to a total of 10 cents for three months.
The point I am making on the COLA clause is that the ceiling the government is putting on that clause should be removed, and I think it should be removed for other employees as well. Why have that cap on at all? As a general proposition it seems to me that it is good not to have a ceiling on it, but in particular in the context of the government's anti-inflation program, if it is going to be successfull, as it claims it will be in reducing the cost of living next year, it has absolutely nothing to fear in terms of the COLA clause proposal of the postal workers. So if its other government policy is successful, it will not lose a cent in removing the cap on the COLA clause. Again it seems to me that that is an item on which a mediator could contribute some advice to both sides.
There are two other issues, but I do not think I will go into details on them. I will simply assert that on the long service pay issue, and on the equal pay for part-time and full-time employees issues, the positions separating the union and the government are not wide apart.
If you look at all these major issues which separate the two parties-major in terms of their concern-you will find two things. First, they are few in number and, second, the distance between the Post Office on the one hand and the postal workers on the other is not great. It therefore seems to me, Madam Speaker, that the proposal I am making tonight for my party, namely, for the appointment of a mediator who would be given a 72-hour mandate to try to bring the two groups together, in the public interest, and to agree on something on a voluntary basis, is reasonable.
Postal Strike
If they do not agree, the mediator would then publish his own recommendations so that the public could make some judgment about the government's attitude and also, in fairness in terms of respecting the impartial nature of the mediator, the proposals should be sent to the trade union membership along with their own bargaining committee's assessment of them.
I think this proposal has a chance of working. I do not want to claim any more than that. It would interfere in a minimal way with the collective bargaining process, and perhaps would have a chance of getting the Post Office back into operation and the postal workers back to work under conditions they might find acceptable.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I must congratulate the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke) for having moved this motion to adjourn to discuss that famous issue of the postal strike, whose study is essential and whose settlement is urgent for all Canadians.
For many years, we have been tackling disastrous strikes, more especially in the civil service. Why? Because we have forgotten the main thing, Madam Speaker, and personally, I have always been convinced that we have been elected to this House to protect the rights of the majority in Canada.
Now in this postal strike, a group of workers, whether they are 20,000, 22,000 or more, are trampling the right of 23 million Canadians to a postal service. The government should therefore require compliance with this right and refrain from walking on a tightrope. On one hand, we hear labour leaders repeat that the minister does not want to resume negotiations while the Postmaster General stated once again today in the House that he is always ready to negotiate.
In all this muddle, who is right and who is wrong? Will government try once more to sit on the fence while avoiding to take the steps that are called for the return to work and that would settle all these disputes once and for all, by creating an arbitration board granted with all appropriate powers of decision.
When will the government cease to make the public pay for its listlessness and its lack of leadership? Why not take a direct action to create and develop suitable and permanent mechanisms to ensure that such crises will not recur continually?
In the Post Office, more than anywhere else, especially in the large centres, due to the number of unions operating inside the postal service, one day we have the truck drivers' strike, another day that of the letter carriers, today it is the postal workers. It is an endless succession of strikes, and that has been going for many years, Madam Speaker.
Who is victimized by all these strikes? The Canadian public. Who could in fact settle all these strikes? None other than the government and union leaders, because they are the ones who have the ability to settle these strikes within the civil service. Madam Speaker, I suggest the government is more than any body responsible for all these strikes which are causing the Canadian economy to deteriorate. We have suggested to the government on a number

November 17, 1975
Postal Strike
of occasions the logical and equitable way to clean up relations within the civil service.
But the government prefers to play the political game and let the Canadian public believe that all the wrongs are on the unions' side. I cannot completely excuse a number of union leaders because, when I consider what is going on, and having talked to a number of postal workers in my own area, I wonder if they really abide by the democratic law which they preach both in respect of the government and their membership, when they insist on a vote by a show of hands whenever the time comes for important decision making such as going on strike.
In order to demonstrate their sincerity, since they claim they are sincere, we can see them all day long on TV to demonstrate their sincerity. Why do these union leaders themselves not propose a secret ballot to the government which is too fearful to step in, Madam Speaker?
When I mention a secret ballot, I am reminded of the New Democratic Party's action. I was very surprised at hon. members of that party opposing the secret ballot. I believe that if there is a way to express one's view freely and democratically, it is through the secret ballot. I wonder why the New Democratic Party members reject such a policy. It is the only way to be fair to everybody and I am convinced-

It is annoying to have ten groups speak at the same time. I would like to be able to finish my speech quietly and my friends who are on the frontbenches will speak all night long if they wish to speak, because we may stay here all night long.
I am sorry; I would like to answer them but my time is too short.
If the minister asked for a secret ballot, I am convinced there would be surprises on both sides, and the Canadian people as a whole would know who is right and who is wrong.
Christmas and New Year are coming and I cannot conceive that the responsible persons on both sides are unable to act loyally, which would end the conflict immediately. Government and union leaders remind me of two teams of wrestlers eager to win but, unlike true professional wres-

tiers who fight legally in a ring, they fight at the expenses of Canadian taxpayers. Madam Speaker, this is what we cannot admit. You will agree with me that this fight is most disgusting. We note that both parties try not to lose face before their members or the public. We know that it might be humiliating for the Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey) to introduce special legislation requiring postal workers to go back to work and we also know that the union leaders secretly hope for such action to disguise their defeat in front of a minister who finds their demands exaggerated. After all, an increase of $1.70 an hour would give postal workers an average hourly salary of $6.26 and this, solely to sort letters, Madam Speaker. To initiate a first agreement they were offered $6.26 an hour. This is acceptable to begin with and I know by experience that many postal workers are ready to accept it, but the leaders require $2.73 an hour, which would yield an average salary of $7.29 an hour.
Let me read you an excerpt from the newspaper Le Quotidien dated November 13 last. I quote:
On the other hand, there will be a waiting period until Mr. Bryce Mackasey returns to Ottawa, although he had not changed his stand on an increase of $1.70 an hour over 30 months. For its part, the union is asking $2.73 over 27 months. The average hourly rate is now $4.56 and the government proposal would increase the annual salary to about $13,000 from now till the end of 1976.
That strikes me as a reasonable start, until better can be achieved. In that way, the people would be given a chance. I go back to the quotation:
Mr. Joe Davidson, president of the Canadian Union of Postal Workers, returning from a visit to southern Ontario branches, stated Tuesday in Ottawa that his union was ready to resume negotiations ...
I believe Mr. Davidson is becoming more lenient. He claims to be willing to resume negotiations. I feel that may mean he will get his members to accept $1.70 initially, because he is convinced, as everyone else today, that most of the postal workers want the strike to end.
In my area, for instance, every rural post office is now open. Employees continue to get their cheques. In rural ridings you do not notice it too much but in large centres where there is no mail that bothers us a bit. Our post offices are open, they are ready, they want this to end and we are told that it is the union leaders who are too radical.
One only has to read the papers to see the number of people who want this strike to end. People say they are prepared to accept the monetary proposals. But there is a dictatorship from union leaders who want to defend the honour of their royalty over their subjects. Union leaders talk strongly about democracy and they are the first ones to care the least about it. Several members want a secret vote to get justice but union bouncers oppose it. Madam Speaker. Why? To develop their famous mail delivery service they set up at $1.25, $1.50 and $2.00 per unit. Will that result in money savings for our fellow citizens who already pay for the postal service? Madam Speaker, where are we going with such a mess? Who has the authority finally here in this Parliament? Would it be Mr. Pepin and all the others, or the minister and the government, or still the cabinet who has the authority? With that feverish fear of a possible reaction at election time, this government shirks all its responsibilities in all areas and we had a striking example of that the other day when we heard the Minister of Finance state that he had no power over the Bank of

Canada. How about that! Today will the Postmaster General refuse to take his responsibilities, to do what everyone expects him to do? Will all departments join that stampede? I hope not, Madam Speaker.
So tonight we are asking this government, in awaiting other solutions, to issue a back to work order and demand a secret vote when a strike is called to protect the individual freedom of all union members who often cannot express themselves at a general meeting for fear of reprisals. speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I join the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke) in wishing the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale), whose advice I miss, renewed health. May I also assure the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra that he was in no way responsible for my illness last Friday. I have a personal responsibility not to sit in the House of Commons one minute longer than I must, if sitting here means wrecking my health. That much, at least, I owe my family.
I could take many avenues in discussing this matter. I could talk to the negotiating team sitting behind me in the gallery, waiting with baited breath for me, perhaps, to tear a strip off them, but that would be a waste of time and effort.
I listened with attention to the philosophy expounded by the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent), much of which I support. We must consider why, in our type of society, we tolerate strikes. I think the Post Office strike has shown from the first week that our people have adjusted to it psychologically. It is amazing how people can adjust, if they think they should for the good of the democratic system. I suggest that is happening in Canada today.
Talking about strikes, I recall Kenneth Galbraith saying one day that the only strike which really bothered him was an elevator strike, because his office was on the forty-fifth floor of the Empire State Building. He said, "Of course, the problem was easy to solve." I asked him what he did. He said he went down to the street and rented an office on the bottom floor.
As someone properly pointed out, new technology is making the Post Office less important for a greater number of Canadians. People are using computer service, new technology, getting by with telex, and using the telephone. We are sending out senior citizen cheques. He might learn that in the conciliation board chairman's report is no inclusion for part-time workers of week-end premiums, something we gladly included, and not through hard bargaining but because it was a social right for regular workers and therefore a social right for part-time workers. This was not included in the conciliation board chairman's report but we extended it to 5,000 part-time workers.
I will be very happy to take that report, which is a very neutral report by a very learned judge, one who was named chairman by both parties, union and management. Perhaps our mistake was trying to improve on it through negotiations instead of simply taking it at this time of anti-inflation, submitting it to the membership, and suggesting that they, like all Canadians, have the good sense to practise a bit of restraint and follow the recommendations of the judge.
Just in case some members may think that the judge's recommendations were harsh, he suggested a 40 hour week, and $1.70 over 30 months with a COLA clause, the same as the other unit. In addition, he introduced a principle that took a lot of persuasion to accept. The principle is that if you regularly work Saturday and Sunday, not overtime but regularly, you are entitled to a premium of 75 cents for Sundays and 60 cents for Saturdays. I wonder how many bus drivers, streetcar drivers-who had to wait around for 15 hours to get in five hours-railway workers, airline workers, or cab drivers get an extra 75 cents an hour for working Sunday and 60 cents an hour for Saturday. This was recommended by the judge. I accepted it in principle. I did not accept the amount, but in negotiation we gave that to the union.
Possibly the main breakthrough in the report of the judge was the clause on automation. The irony is that the Postmaster General who is now being classed as reactionary brought in that particular clause in private industry.
The union said they had to have this clause if they were going to continue working in the Post Office.
We all remember "Boycott the Postal Code". That was the slogan. We all remember the union leaders telling us how effective the boycott was, and how they had nullified automation. They are sitting up there. They will tell you they were able to offset automation by boycotting the postal code. It is significant that, despite the fact that nowhere in the public service does such a provision exist, this judge felt it logical, proper, and moral in this day and age that workers be protected against the effects of technology, a view I share.

It is significant that Treasury Board in its wisdom agreed to include in this collective agreement complete and utter protection against the effects of technology when introduced by management, namely, a clause which says you must notify them, the union, in writing in ample time so that they can prepare to accept or reject the right to negotiate and then, if after so many days no settlement is reached, the matter goes to arbitration. I think there is a limit of 15 days within which the arbitrator must bring back a settlement, as in the case of the railways.
So in addition to the COLA clause which is unique in the public service, in addition to the weekend premiums which are unique virtually anywhere in Canada, you have this unique provision protecting public servants against the effects of automation. Indeed, they have complete security against lay-offs due to lack of business. I would like to include one day in our collective agreement provisions which would allow the Postmaster General of the day to have his work staff fluctuate with the volume of mail which comes in. Then you might get an efficient Post Office.

I might remind the postal workers and the union leaders that they have lost the equivalent of 3,500 man-year positions due to their illegal work stoppages over the last five years. They have yet to lose a single job through automation. Are we asking these workers to make a sacrifice? Do you think negotiations began in October? The hon. gentleman has gone to lick his wounds, but that is all right.
I want to make it clear that my objective is still to arrive at a negotiated settlement. On November 9, on television, in answer to a question I said on the issue of part time workers, which the hon. gentleman mentioned tonight, that we could begin negotiations there and then, that very evening. The trouble with this negotiating team is they never know when they've got a good bargain or when they have a good deal. They cannot seem to understand there does come a moment where there is just no more money to give them. If they think they are going to sit down tomorrow with a mediator, the Postmaster General or anybody representing the government, and end up with a settlement for less then 40 hours a week, or more than $1.70 an hour, for a shorter period than 30 months, they are dreaming in technicolour.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext: That is true whether the strike lasts a day, a week, a month or a year. It is a matter of principle here. We argue in this House sometimes about private enterprise. I think we all agree that sometimes there is bad management of business. You can get bad landlords, which means rent controls. You can get bad leadership.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext: And bad government!

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext:
This has been going on since last January. Just in case anybody thinks that the bargaining unit- and I am not including myself as Postmaster General- cannot negotiate, take the case of the other union, the
November 17, 1975

letter carriers. They began bargaining in January. They bargained for a certain period of time, they went to a conciliation board, they bargained and went to mediation, and in June they arrived at what they considered to be the best collective agreement they had ever obtained, an agreement which was ratified by 82 per cent of the membership.
This union came in in March with a demand emanating from a union newspaper. Coupled with this demand were certain prerequisites, as they called them. Before they would even start negotiating we had to convert the Post Office into a Crown corporation. They also wanted an immediate raise of $1 an hour before they would even begin negotiating, plus one or two minor items. Finally, after getting through the conciliation officer stage in June, which at least brought in their demands, they got to the conciliation board stage in September-October-about then-and, as I mentioned, the Public Service Staff Relations Board named Jules Moisan of the Quebec Superior Court as chairman. This was after getting both parties to agree to the judge.
Because so little had been accomplished as a result of this harassment, this demand that the Post Office become a Crown corporation before negotiations could take place, it took that poor gentleman eight weeks of constant discussion with both parties in order to arrive at what is known as the Moisan report-the report of the chairman of that board. It was not a unanimous report; it was not even a majority report in the sense that we agreed only in principle to the weekend premium without putting any monetary value on it. It is wrong to say our position was inflexible since our first position was $1.15 for 32 months and did not include weekend premiums or specific benefit for part-time workers. We were very flexible, Madam Speaker.
I realize there are others who wish to speak, and there is a vote coming on pretty soon. I do not wish to continue afterward, but I might say that by April 24 there had been no less than eight meetings with that union. Finally, in July, they met with the conciliation officer and it was July 21 before they even sat down to hear the terms of reference. The conciliation board worked from August 18 to October 7 and negotiated from October 16 to November 6. People might ask, "How come there was a strike?" The answer is very simple. While we were negotiating in good faith, the union, because it did not have a strike mandate- and I say that publicly and as an honourable gentleman of this House-arranged in the dead of night with the minority in the major cities to set up picket lines so that the silent majority, the older workers, the responsible Canadians who only want to earn their living like anybody else, found themselves confronted when they went to the workplace with picket lines they did not dare cross.
What was the advantage to the membership to go on strike in the middle of negotiations? We in the government have no right to lock out. There was no particular advantage other than frighten off the majority of workers who were more than happy with the report of the conciliation chairman if through some legal means they could have had an opportunity of expressing that opinion.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I presume somebody else on the other side will be able to take up where the Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey) left off. I do not want to escalate any controversy tonight; I hope to make a quiet contribution, if I may. It did seem to me that the Postmaster General was threshing over some recent history rather than telling the House what he proposes to do in the present emergency. We start off from a common position.
Mr. Speaker, if some of those fellows with louder voices and keener minds would keep quiet for a few minutes, we could perhaps make a little progress. I might suggest that this is the kind of controversy in which a little reason and a little less heat might produce a little more light.
We start off with the position that parliament has given the postal workers the right to strike. But all parties in the House recognize that there comes a point when the public interest must prevail and that the right to strike should be curtailed or modified in the particular situation. I think we agree that serious damage is being done as the strike continues. There is great inconvenience; there is perhaps irreparable harm being done to certain agencies, such as that well known charitable agency that depends very heavily upon the sale of Christmas seals. There is no need to document the damage that is being done.
I might remind the Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey) that not everyone is in the position in which John Kenneth Galbraith found himself, that when he could not reach his accommodation on the fortieth floor he went down the street and rented some other accommodation. It is not everyone who can make up for the lack of a postal service by sending telegrams or using the telephone. If I may borrow a phrase commonly used by the Postmaster General, res ipsa loquitur.
The strike is continuing, with the main issue being the demand for rates of pay-I want to make sure I state it correctly-which are higher than the government says its anti-inflationary program will permit. In other words, the government's guidelines do not restrict the right to strike in this instance, but the government's anti-inflationary guidelines certainly circumscribe the scope of collective bargaining. So that when the government says it is a question of balancing the public interest against interference with free collective bargaining, we in this House must take note that the government, in the name of the public interest, has already taken a position in its fight against inflation and introduced legislation to limit increases in pay for which any labour union can bargain. I say it is

November 17, 1975
Postal Strike
proposing limits on the right to collective bargaining for a far longer period than I find acceptable.
The union is seeking increases that are higher than the government says its guidelines will permit. The purpose of the continuing strike essentially is to persuade the government to accept a bigger increase than its guidelines permit. So it is really pretty silly, if I may speak frankly and bluntly, for the government to say that it does not want to interfere with the collective bargaining process, because it has already done that.
I also say it is pretty silly for the government to refuse to restore the postal service to the Canadian people, pretending that it is preserving the legal right of the union which it has already modified. Leaving aside for a moment the question whether the right to strike in essential services should be modified, and leaving aside for a moment all the difficulties that any such question raises or that any such position brings forward, the fact is that the anti-inflationary guidelines have been adopted by the government indicating a firm determination by the government to limit the scope of collective bargaining in so far as wage and salary increases are concerned. In these circumstances, it surely is close to hypocrisy for the government to say that it will not ask parliament to order a return to work, when the government has already decreed there is no way in which the union can get the higher wages it is striking for.
I have to ask myself whether there is not another motive for the position that the government is taking. Is the government refusing to ask parliament to intervene because doing so would in some way take the union off the hook? Is the government insisting that, despite all the damage being done to the public, the union has to be made to learn that it has to accept responsibility here? Parliament would not be letting the union off the hook if there was a back to work direction given by parliament, because any such order would be within the anti-inflationary guidelines of the government.
If the government is serious about holding to its guidelines it, the government, has to place the union on the hook-if we are going to talk about someone being on a hook. It is not a question of parliament taking the union off the hook. All of us in the House, including the government, have to recognize that the government has, by adopting its guidelines, placed the union on a hook and proposes to keep it there during the life of its wage and price guidelines program. So there is no question of taking the union off the hook.
Is the government's concern that parliament might take the union executive off the hook? The leaders of this union may not be very popular. It may be popular for the government to attack them; I do not know. But the public is certainly fed up with disruptions in postal service. Surely it is not our business in parliament, and it is not the business of the government, to try to break a union executive and to put the public to great loss and inconvenience in the process.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I was interrupted by the bell for the vote I was emphasizing that the government had already substantially restricted the scope of collective bargaining as a result of its anti-inflationary program, and that consequently it was very close to hypocrisy for the government to refrain from taking any action or put any measure before parliament, on the grounds that this would interfere with a right given to the postal workers by parliament when, as a matter of general policy, the government had expressed its determination that the scope of collective bargaining would be limited during the course of its control program, and had made it very clear that there was no way in which the union could get more than had been offered to them.
I therefore had to ask myself what the real motive was for the government's failure to act. It cannot be explained on the ground that a return to work order by parliament would take the union off the hook, because the government has already placed the union on a hook that will last as long as the control programs are in place. I had to ask myself therefore what the reason was for the government's behaviour, the reason for the Postmaster General's reiteration of the position here tonight that a good long strike would be a good thing. I do not want to misquote him or misinterpret him, but that is what I understood him to say-that a good long strike would be a good thing for the country. In the circumstances I had to ask whether the reason for this was the desire of the government to break the union executive, and incidentally to put the public to great loss and inconvenience in the process.
There certainly have been cases of government intervention in the management and operation of unions. In some

instances unions have been put into trusteeship. Is the government in this instance trying to accomplish through the pressure of a long strike what it is not prepared to do openly? If the government lets things go on until Easter, if the government encourages continuance of a strike of these postal employees until Easter, as the minister says he is prepared to do, the government may very well destroy the union executive, and perhaps the union itself, and would certainly also destroy a lot of Canadian people in the process.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext: While John Kenneth Galbraith may be able to look after himself, there are a lot of Canadians who cannot look after themselves.

There has been discussion about the advisability of a vote. The hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) put forward a constructive motion this afternoon which the government accepted. The leader of the New Democratic party this evening suggested that was an unwarranted intervention, that there was no legal authority to do it in the first place, that it was an unwarranted intervention in the affairs of the union, and he then proposed a modification of this which the Postmaster General, in his turn, ridiculed. I had the impression from what has been said, and from my own background, that any question could be put to the membership of the union either only with the approval of the executive or by a change in legislation. That would be the case whether it is the proposal of the leader of the New Democratic Party or the proposal of the hon. member for St. John's East and legislation would be required.
The leader of the New Democratic Party did not indicate whether the union accepted his proposal. I assume he was not speaking with the authority or approval of the union. I want to say I feel certain that, if there is a way of getting a vote of the membership on a reasonable proposition within a reasonable period of time, parliament and the people of Canada would be prepared to wait for that.
I do not want to be unfair but I do not think the Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey) indicated this evening that he would take constructive action to settle this issue. He had plenty of time, although there was not enough time for him to review the last ten years of postal negotiations and tell the House what he intends to do.
In summary I say, as my time is nearly finished, that we should do all we can to bring before the membership this question in a fair way, in order that there may be a vote. If that cannot be done, if legislation for accomplishing that purpose must be introduced, then in the national interest the government should ask parliament to order a return to work, with a provision for continued negotiation for limited time. I repeat what I said several times previously. It is sheer hypocrisy, or close to it, for the government to say it cannot do that because it would be an intervention in the collective bargaining process; after all, the government has already intervened drastically. It has limited the scope of
November 17, 1975

collective bargaining by adopting and being determined to enforce its guidelines.

What did the hon. member say about inflation? I think he made on reference to the Anti-Inflation Board. He said he hoped that the solution, whatever it may be, would be arrived at voluntarily, and would be referred to the AntiInflation Board. He said that there is one thing wrong with the Post Office-its managers do not have the guts to charge enough for their services. He said that first class letters should cost 25 cents to send. I ask, what will this do to the pensioners, the people about whom the hon. member's colleague-I give him full marks for his concern-is worried? Will he support a union whose leader says that first class mail in this country should cost 25 cents to send? Is he prepared to see that done? Is he prepared to side with the union whose leader has said on tape and in front of the television camera, "The public be damned!'' Has the hon. member not one critical word to say about that union?

Mr. Speaker, I call this an irresponsible strike, a challenge to parliament's attempt to deal with inflation. There is a danger that the public will force parliament to pass legislation which will be a reaction to this strike, and that would be unfortunate indeed. The members of this House and of the other place who sit on the special joint committee have a serious responsibility in weighing recommendations to be made, for we must avoid that situation, and make sure that legislation is passed only if it is absolutely necessary.
I made the suggestion to the committee that before a legal strike could take place the Public Service Staff Relations Board should conduct a vote on the final offer of the employer and that the board should be responsible for certifying the results of that vote. I know there are problems with any suggestion of this nature. I know it will be opposed by members of the New Democratic Party, among others, but they have to answer to the people of Canada what we are going to do to stop a union executive that will not allow the employer's final offer to be voted upon in a free and secret ballot.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to the speech made by the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis) who, just a few moments ago, indicated the proposal he made to the joint committee on employer-employee relations. I do not want in any way to detract from the hon. member's interest in that subject because I know it is sincere. However, it is my understanding that that proposal was first made in a public way by the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale), who cannot be here this evening. When the opportunity comes to deal with the matter, which I hope will be shortly, I intend to support it. That kind of principle will guarantee that which I suspect has

not taken place within the postal union, that is, the opportunity for the rank and file of the union to consider in a free and open way the offer that has been made to it.
I want to talk for a few moments about the speech made by the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent). He talked about mediation. It may be a useful exercise, perhaps not. The hon. member asked us to consider the position of the union. He castigated the government. Not once did he ask us to consider the public interest.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext:
The emphasis of his speech was the preservation of the right to strike. That is an important right, but it should not override the public interest. We should not lose track of the importance of that.
I do not want to suggest that in terms of attitude the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby is the only one who can be faulted. Some blame has to be laid at the feet of the Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey). It was he who said in this House "Let's have one good strike and have it over with." In effect he was saying small business be damned, senior citizens be damned, people who depend on investment income be damned. I put him in no better position with respect to that statement in terms of leadership than the president of the union who said the public be damned.
A few moments ago some speakers called for leaderhips. I do not want to be unkind to the Postmaster General. In the history of this whole matter with regard to the bringing together of the parties and the settlement of the dispute there has been at least a modicum of a lack of leadership on both sides.
The purpose of the motion tonight is not to call one another names. That is not productive. It is to give encouragement to the government on one hand, and to the union members on the other, with regard to the settlement of the dispute. It is to say to the leadership of the union that this parliament does not approve of any tactic which deprives the members of the union of the right to deal with an offer that has been made by management. That is a very important matter.
The hon. member for Ottawa West did not mention the complete position put forward by this party to-night. I call his attention to the admirable speech made by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) who made it clear that this party wants, first of all, that the union membership have the right to a free vote. I do not think that there is any doubt about that in this House. If there is, let that member stand up and say so. The government ought to take this into consideration, not in two weeks, but now. If that fails, having regard to the importance of the public service and the postal service in the public interest, it is important that the government face up to the fact that the alternative, which we would all regret, is putting the union back to work. That position was put fairly carefully by the two people who have spoken thus far in this party.
This evening I received a call from a member of the postal union in the town of Prescott. There are seven members in that bargaining unit. The scrutineer called and told me that a vote was taken on October 10, 1975. They had two ballots, one of which asked "Do you accept the
November 17, 1975

proposed collective agreement?". The second ballot asked "Do you support the recommendations of your negotiating committee?" or words to that effect. They were told that they were not to use the first ballot which would have put before that local, which is symbolic of a number of locals in this country, the question as to whether the government offer was good. This is what I have been told.
Still, they were told to vote on the second question, whether they supported the recommendation of the negotiating committee which was not to accept the offer made by the government. So they voted, this small local; there are seven of them in it. Six voted not to support the recommendations of the negotiating committee, and there was one spoiled ballot. That local was immediately decertified.

speechtext: Oh, oh!

They were told that as a result of that vote the union was authorized to continue in the position it had taken, because they had the executive committee and the negotiating committee authorization to deal only with the minority report. But the first question had never been submitted to the union membership, that question being: Do you accept the government's offer? That is the position of the local at Prescott. If that is the position of the local at Prescott, the question in my mind is: what is the position of locals across the country, and what would be the result if the government decided to move in the next little while and presented its last and final offer to the union membership?
In my submission, it would do two things: it would preserve democracy in the union, which is self-evidently not there at the moment, and it would probably lead to a return to work or at least to an overwhelming vote to return to work. I think this is worthy of the government's attention. Parliament is always in the position of being able to legislate them back to work, in any event.
What we see here is a spillover which could affect the public service far behond the right to strike in the postal service. I hear people suggesting we should do away completely with the right to strike in the public service, even though some of those who talk about such an eventuality cannot define what an essential service is; it is an extremely difficult area and one which the Finkelman committee is presently considering. I would point out that the record as far as public service bargaining is concerned has been pretty good except for the Post Office. I, for one, do not want rights which were given by parliament to be taken away unceremoniously, or even to hear people demanding that this be done because of the irresponsibility of the leadership of one union.

I do not wish to take up the time of the House unduly. The minister knows I regard public service bargaining as a complex matter, one not to be trifled with by people who wish to make a big show going around the country saying, "Let's get rid of the right to strike." The right to strike and the process of collective bargaining have been sanctioned by parliament. Before we take it away, I think we should let the main beneficiaries, in this case the postal workers, cast their votes-and if it takes a bill to do it, bring one in-on whether to accept the offer made to them by the government. I do not know whether that offer is right or wrong, too high or too low. In any case, it is subject to review by the Anti-Inflation Board. The minister nods his head.
Subject to all these considerations, to the extent it can having regard to the government's program, the membership ought to have the right to decide and the government ought to move quickly to give them that right.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like many backbenchers on this side of the House I am glad to speak on the motion before us tonight. I am particularly happy to speak on the motion, first, to put my own views squarely on the record and, second and more important, to demonstrate the extent of the support members on our side of the House are giving to our Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey), a man who has endangered his health and who has put his career on the line in the interests of achieving a fair, equitable settlement for a group of workers who have seen their incomes fall drastically behind over the past few years.
The first fight in this battle took place last spring when members of our caucus supported the Postmaster General in his attempt to convince Treasury Board that the letter carriers deserved a general salary increase. We agreed with him and argued that postal employees must be given the financial remuneration they had historically earned in the interests of restoring a measure of pride and dignity to an often maligned vocation. We won that fight and the leadership of the Letter Carriers Union is to be praised for its responsible deportment throughout the negotiations and for its part in arriving at a settlement.
It goes without saying that this general settlement should be extended to cover the other half of the postal employees, the inside workers as they are known. But here the problem became complicated. The minister was faced by an irresponsible president of the Canadian Union of Postal Workers-I hope he is still here tonight to hear what some of us feel about him-and an equally irresponsible chief negotiator for the union. He found himself dealing with two men whose personal ideological and political views superseded the best interests of those they were supposed to represent at the bargaining table. As a result we face a situation in which a fair settlement is sitting on that table, the majority of the postal workers across the country ready to accept its generous terms, yet their leaders are afraid to submit the package to a national vote. If there is a better example of trade unionist
9150

November 17, 1975
Postal Strike
totalitarianism and demagoguery, I defy members of the House to show me one.
Members on this side of the House are not anti-union. In fact if the members of the NDP did their homework they would find that two out of every four labour votes in this country go to the Liberal party. We have, historically, spoken for the workers. We are not anti-union, but we are against the demagoguery, the totalitarianism and the irresponsibility we find in our trade unions in Canada today.
The trouble is that Mr. Davidson is a product of a political culture which is radically different from the political culture in this country. He is a product of an anarchist strain evident over the past century on the Clydeside docks. As Freud saw everything through sexual eyeglasses, Mr. Davidson, like his mentor, Karl Marx, sees all political debate through the eyeglasses of class struggle and social strife.
There has been no tradition of class warfare in this country. We are all equal. We are all workers, not members of an upper class, middle class, or working class. Workers and management should be able to use the collective bargaining process without manipulation from those like the president of the Canadian Union of Postal Workers who try to impose their own political values upon a reasonable attempt to settle this dispute.
I feel I can take Mr. Davidson to task, Mr. Speaker. I was born in his country. I have studied in his country and I have worked there. I have seen the havoc wreaked upon the British economy by irresponsible trade union leadership, the trade union leadership elites that we see today. I do not want to see the same values, these destructive beliefs, transferred to the labour situation in this country.
What of the chief negotiator for the union, a man whose obviously unbending views cannot but lead one to the conclusion that he has an interest in sabotaging not only these particular postal negotiations but also the collective bargaining process in general. Perhaps-I say "perhaps", Mr. Speaker, because I am loth to utter this-he seeks to subvert the very essence and very fibre of the total political structure in this country through his ruminations and histrionics at the bargaining table.
The negotiators have asked for a 71 per cent salary increase. This has been scaled down. The Postmaster General bargained in good faith. Before monetary matters were to be discussed, the union wanted to discuss the effects of automation, and we negotiated. They wanted to discuss electronic surveillance, and we negotiated. They wanted to discuss casual labour, and we negotiated that too. Then when we wanted to get down to monetary matters, the bread and butter issues-as the Postmaster General has said, the average member of the Canadian Union of Postal Workers, the average worker in this country, just wants enough money to eat and give him a good standard of living-the union came along and threw in yet another bone of contention, a cost of living clause and a reduction in the work week. How many more minor issues do we have to settle before we get down to the principal issue of money?
Consistently this bargaining team has avoided the very generous settlement proposed. I need not go into the

details, but it is 38 per cent, $1.70 an hour over 30 months, a settlement that exceeds the government's anti-inflation guidelines. What is this team negotiating? What is it avoiding? Why, as has been said earlier, do they not submit this settlement to a national vote?
I see the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broad-bent) is not here to face the rest of the music this evening, but he castigated the Postmaster General for advocating a deviation from normal bargaining procedure by wanting the union membership to vote on the pay offer. He is right; it is a deviation from the normal bargaining procedure. But the union and the union's negotiating team have deviated from the normal bargaining procedure from the very beginning of these negotiations. In fact the chief negotiator and his associates have been downright devious in their behaviour throughout.
So we have the spectre of these two gentlemen, a latter day vaudeville team or Pied Piper team, going on their own merry way without regard for the thousands of helpless members they are leading into debt each day this dispute continues. It is the spectre of two men on full union pay of some $18,000 to $19,000 a year, twice as much as an average postal worker makes, hob-nobbing across this country, flying, I am told, in first-class accommodation on Air Canada, eating and drinking from an apparently inexhaustible expense account paid for by the sweat of the members whom they dare say they represent. What a charade! What an injustice!
This ineffectual motion before us expresses timid concern but shies away from a substantive recommendation. I see the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke) has also left. He is a hard-working fellow. He is amiable-I know him well-and he is respected by many in this House. However, tonight it appears that he and the others of his party who support this motion are ambivalent.
My colleague, the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis), analysed the motion and asked what members of the opposition really wanted. What do they want? Do they want to give the workers more money? Or are they asking the government to introduce legislation forcing the postal employees back to work? The hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) talks about showing concern for the public interest. That is a lovely phrase. But because they do not have the obligation to govern, hon. members opposite do not have to be specific and tell us what we should do. If they want the government to shoot holes in its anti-inflation program by awarding the postal workers more money, let them say it. If they want back-to-work legislation, let them say it. But let them not introduce a namby-pamby, wishy-washy motion like the one before us which is keeping us up well past our bedtime.
Let me tell you, Mr. Speaker, why the members on this side are firm about not legislating the workers back to their jobs. We do not want to give the union bargaining team and its leadership the easy way out; it is as simple as that. This strike could have been avoided. We did not want a strike. The president of the Toronto local is one of my constituents, a very reasonable fellow. I have been besieged by calls from members of the union. They do not want to strike, but they are intimidated. That is what we have today, Mr. Speaker. It is not a question of fighting against trade unionism. You would have to be a fool to
November 17, 1975

argue the merits of trade union activity and the benefits trade unions have brought to society.

speechtext: The hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke) is here now.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS

Good; I hope he is listening. What we are really arguing about is the subversion of the trade union movement, and inadvertently the subversion of democracy. We do not only have to talk about this dispute; we can talk about the longshoremen's dispute where union leaders in this country defied parliament, or tried to defy parliament. Once we settle this dispute we have to get down to serious thought about improving labour relations. But I stress this can be done only after we settle this dispute. As far as I am concerned-and I am sure I speak for most of the members on this side-it will be a long way to go before we want to give parliament a job that it should not really be doing by legislating the postal workers back to work.
The real solution here lies with the workers. As each day passes, I am sure that more of them will go back to work. More will decide that to work and earn a living and accept a generous settlement is better than sitting on the sidelines while their leaders provoke great dissent and discussion across the land at the cost of the average worker. There is no doubt that the Postmaster General's stand has the full support of the people in the metropolitan Toronto area from which I come. It is also quite evident to me that workers in the Toronto area, and probably in other parts of the country, do not want to stay on strike any longer; they would love to accept the wage offer.
I could go on and on but would only be repeating what has already been said, and I know there are more speakers. If this union's leaders really had the guts to submit this offer to its workers, then they would be worthy of showing leadership and could be praised. But they are not giving this kind of leadership. They are not interested in a settlement. As I have said before, I hope members of this side hang tough over the next two or three weeks, or however long it takes.
You can talk about small businessmen over there as much as you like, but they are learning to adjust.

Mr. Speaker, as the proposer of this motion I rise on a point of order. I listened very intently to the remarks of the hon. member for York
Postal Strike
East (Mr. Collenette). He said some disparaging things about the content of this motion. Let me suggest that he might read the motion and the Standing Order under which it is proposed, since the purport of the content of the motion is simply that this House do now adjourn.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the one hand the credit must of course go to my party for making it possible to take part in this emergency debate this evening. On the other hand it is a sad state of affairs indeed when parliamentarians once again have to digress from the regular day-to-day proceedings of the House of Commons and force themselves to discuss the problem of yet another strike. I say sad, because if the government had a half decent policy to deal with strikes in general, particularly those in essential services such as the Post Office, it would not have to depend on any special motions or Standing Orders such as this, and a majority of work stoppages could be prevented.
It is clear to see that the government not only does not have a half decent policy relating to work stoppages, but it in fact has no policy whatsoever to deal with these destructive strikes which bring many of our industries to their knees, and just as many small businessmen to a tragic end.
I do not have to expound on the fact that a strike like the one we are facing today threatens the very existence of small businesses in Canada, the existence of which has become a vital part of our over-all economy, as it is the small businessman who forms the backbone of our economic and industrial way of life, regardless of what the Liberal speaker before me said.
By allowing this strike to continue and by not presenting a comprehensive program encompassing the whole, general, broad area of exorbitant union demands, we will only assist in the complete destruction of the economy of this country. I should like to point out, however, that the Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey) has at least taken the honorable step of sticking firmly to his final monetary offer as far as this strike is concerned. Whether we legislate the CUPW back to work, which I personally would support wholeheartedly, or we wait for events to run their own course, or whatever, there is no question but that after much suffering by all Canadians, including the union members, at one point or another the mail will again flow and we will be back to square one. That is the sad thing, Mr. Speaker.
We will be back to square one waiting for another union, perhaps in the same service, to bring the nation to an economic standstill once again. We will be back to square one without having solved one solitary long-term issue, and that is my point. That is what is so frustrating about the government which deals with a problem on a temporary basis while at the same it allows unions to build long-term unprecedented strength. The only ones who benefit are those tough union leaders, some of whom are here this evening, who receive their incentives from who Knows what infiltrators.
It would not be as tragic if, as a result of union power, the productivity in our country were increased, but unfortunately the fact of the matter is that while increases in labour wages continue to rise higher than any other wages
