in the industrialized world, productivity in Canada has decreased by nearly 10 per cent per year. What better example could there be of inflation? The deficit in the Post Office, with all the union demands, can only be matched by that of the mayor of Montreal and his Olympic Games. In 1973 the Post Office had a deficit of $90 million, and in the last year that increased to over $320 million.
Again this would not be as serious if the postal service were at least adequate, but it seems to me the original natives of this country hundreds of years ago had a more reliable system of communication with smoke signals than we have through the Post Office today. I believe this is an obvious case of taking advantage of those who cannot fight for themselves but must depend on strong government intervention, intervening fairly on their behalf.
I am referring not only to small businessmen, whom I mentioned earlier, but to the two-thirds of the Canadian labour force which is not unionized. What about the large portion of the union membership who do not approve of their leaders, and there are many, and are either afraid to disapprove openly or who, in more cases than not, find their union votes are usually misrepresented and sometimes not counted at all because of the all too obvious voting irregularities that exist in a great many union halls in Canada today?
What seems to be the problem? There are many, and the first one is quite obvious. Look at the number of unions within some of the essential sectors of our economy. The Post Office, in fact, has five different unions. The problem, as I say, is obvious. Any one of those unions can force a strike within its own sector, just like the present strike by CUPW now taking place within the Post Office. It is an unfortunate possibility that after a settlement is finalized and the Post Office re-opens, the letter carriers will perhaps see fit to go on strike and thus bring the Post Office once again to a standstill, and we will have accomplished nothing.
The same is true in respect of the air transport industry with 15 different unions; 16 unions are involved in handling grain in this country, 21 different unions are involved in the rail service, and 35 at various ports.
Keeping this fragmentation of union power in mind I was happy to introduce a bill last July for the purpose of having union groups in a single public service sector bargaining with the Treasury Board simultaneously, and having contracts negotiated to run for a duration of three years. This would assure the taxpaying public that each essential public service sector would be strike free except for the possibility of a walk-out every three years.
In this regard I was pleased to note in a confidential memorandum to cabinet, prepared by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) some months ago, recommendations along the line which I proposed in that bill. I would be more than pleased to withdraw my own bill in favour of a government bill dealing with the subject matter or, indeed, any legislative proposals that would help keep our economy on an even keel, but it seems quite obvious that the government is not prepared to move at all, let alone in that direction.
Even with the concept of single sector bargaining, however, further steps could be taken to limit labour disrup-

tions while at the same time preserving fairness to labour. Therefore last March I presented another private bill based on the Taft-Hartley Act. This bill would give the Governor in Council the right to bring a strike or lock-out to an end on a temporary basis if such a strike or lock-out, in the opinion of the Governor in Council, would adversely affect the national or public interest if it continued. Such an order would naturally expire upon the execution of a collective agreement, and the strikers would be free to walk out on the expiry of their own agreement.
Lastly, I was able to introduce a bill today which in plain and simple terms would on a temporary basis, and I emphasize "temporary basis", take away the right to strike in the essential services of our economy for the duration of the government's Anti-Inflation Act, now at the committee stage.
If anyone thinks the anti-inflation program enunciated by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) last month can work on its own merit without amendments, he or she had better think again. Unless there are a number of changes made during the committee state I, for one, will be forced to vote against that bill when it comes back to the House.
There is no question but that the time has come for decisive government action regarding the multitude of strikes which continue to plague our country. The time has come not just for a temporary end to one strike but for a comprehensive program to deal with the loss of productivity due to strikes and walkouts on a long-term basis. We will not exist much longer as a viable industrial nation if we continue to take this ad hoc approach to strikes that the government is asking us to accept as a way of life.
In the last fiscal year, for example, there were 177,000 man-days lost as a result of strikes in the Post Office alone. That figure has already more than doubled as a result of the current work stoppage in the Post Office. In the last two fiscal years there were over 100,000 man-days lost in air transport, close to one million man-days lost in the rail service, and over l'/2 million man-days lost as a result of strikes solely by employees under the jurisdiction of the federal government. This, Mr. Speaker, cannot be and is not a healthy sign of things to come under the present Liberal administration.
My fervent wish as a member of parliament and as a concerned citizen of this great country is that we parliamentarians get off our butts, leave party politics on the sidelines, and resolve a just and comprehensive settlement to this and future labour disputes that would benefit all Canadians.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the best proof members of parliament could have that a new start must be made if a settlement of the strike is to take place is the speech the Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey) made tonight, because if ever there was a speech in which a minister was inflexible, obstinate, and self-righteous, this was it.
The minister preened himself on the fact that he has never made a mistake and is right in the final offer he made about a month ago, even though two months ago he was not prepared to offer a whole host of concessions
November 17, 1975

which he offered in the final days before the strike started, and in the three or four days after it started. So if ever there was proof that the minister has lost his ability to be objective in an effort to settle the dispute which is inconveniencing all the people of Canada, and which is causing great difficulty to so many people in Canada, it was the speech the minister made. I could hardly believe my ears when I heard the minister say the public is adjusting quite easily to the strike and that people are not suffering.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext: He did not say that.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext:
Yes; he said precisely that. He said the people have not been disturbed by the strike which has already gone on for a month. He said the strike could go on until Christmas, and indeed until Easter. On Friday, because my plane was late leaving for Winnipeg, I had to wait at the airport. While I was there I sat beside a businessman who told me that he is spending $100 a day on courier service. I did some arithmetic. I admit that my arithmetic is not very good but, calculating it on the basis of roughly 200 working days, it seems to me that that businessman has an expense now in the neighbourhood of over $20,000 a year. I think he is doing reasonably well, but he is not in a position to carry a burden of that kind. If the minister is talking about a strike lasting until Easter he is talking about a figure close to half that sum.
I also spoke to a businessman in my city. He has a mail order business. He deals in electrical appliances, radios, washing machines, and similar equipment. He has done virtually no business for the last month. It is all very well for the minister to say that businessmen are adjusting. It may be that Eatons, The Bay and Simpsons-Sears are adjusting quite well, -but that businessman in Winnipeg, and I am sure many others like him, are not in a position to do business.
My friend, the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas), just told me about the people of Vancouver Island who grow holly for sale in places like California. They usually receive their orders by mail and send out their holly C.O.D. by mail. They are not receiving any orders, and if they did they would not know how to fill them. The Postmaster General has made up his mind that people can live with the strike for six months. He can manage. The government has a telephone system, a telex system and couriers. It can manage. That does not mean the ordinary citizens can manage. It certainly does not mean they can afford the effect of a strike which need not have occurred, and which ought not to be continuing.
We heard a very impassioned speech by the hon. member for York East (Mr. Collenette). He talked about what "we" had done to try to settle the strike. I suppose he was using the word we in a loyal party sense because I did not know that backbench members of parliament, especially government members like him who sit so far back I can hardly see them, were involved in the negotiations. I do not know how he knew that the President of the Canadian Union of Postal Workers is a stubborn man. He may be; I do not know. Neither of us were involved in the negotiations.
I suggest it takes two stubborn people to make an argument. If the union leaders have been stubborn, and they may have been-I have not been involved in the negotiations and do not know what they are doing but I do know
Postal Strike
what the Postmaster General has been doing-I know the Postmaster General has been very busy both inside and outside this House. If ever a cabinet minister curried favour of the representatives of the media it is this Postmaster General who sees them every half hour if he can, and gives them his side of the story. That is what we get through the media.
I do not say that the government is wrong or the union is right, but if ever there was a campaign to vilify a group of people it is that carried on by the Postmaster General against the union. One would think that the Post Office has been generous, that it was quick in making an offer, that the offer was a good offer, and that the union and workers rejected it out of hand.
We could go back almost ten years to the first stoppage. It was an illegal stoppage because there was no legislation permitting a strike in 1966. In 1966 the postal workers were illegally on strike. Any strike in which they would be involved at that time would be illegal. The Liberal government of the day appointed a judge from Quebec, Judge Montpetit, to look into the operations of the Post Office. There are several recommendations which were made by Judge Montpetit in 1966 which still have not been implemented by the Post Office under the leadership of this so-called friend of labour in 1975. Is it any wonder the postal workers, and not just their leaders, are unhappy with the government and the department?
Let me refer the parliamentary secretary to the Globe and Mail issue of Monday, November 10, which on its front page has the lead story entitled "Interference by other departments hampers Post Office, memo says". Who is the memo by? Not by that flaming radical, the president of the postal workers, not by the vice-president who has been heading the negotiation. It is written by the assistant deputy Postmaster-General, Mr. J. E. Uberig.
Let me just put on the record a couple of paragraphs from that report which he made to the Postmaster General and which the Postmaster General, in his desire to fight the postal workers' union probably filed in the not-to-be-read-for-a-year-from-now filing cabinet. I want to read that because some of us say that the Post Office Department and the minister are not entirely free of blame for this impasse to which we have come. The article in the Globe and Mail reads:
Post Office Act states that the Postmaster General shall administer, superintend and manage the Post Office.
This seems to be a simple enough authority, but a number of other acts have superimposed effects on the operations of the Post Office, so as to give certain authorities to other ministers of the government or to limit severely the ability of the Postmaster General (and through him the department) in dealing with problems-
Problems arise not only with wage arrangements for blue-collar workers (e.g. reluctance to entertain concept of buy-back of sick leave accruals), but also with management (e.g. tardiness in establishing new pay rates for managerial exclusions-
The article goes on:
-"the needs of a major portion of the postal employees who are in a blue-collared, industrial-type setting" because it does not allow bargaining on such items as technological change, classifications and other issues.

Postal Strike
The author of the memo is saying this in connection with his analysis that the postal worker should come out of the jurisdiction of the Public Service Staff Relations Act and be included among the workers who come under the provisions of the revised Canada Labour Code.
I could go on, but there you have evidence from a senior official in the Post Office Department that the Post Office in its present set-up cannot do the" job which it is required to do. Let us not talk about what this man says, or what Judge Monpetit said. Let us go back to about a year and a half ago when the operation of the automatic sorting machines was coming on stream.
What was the rate set by the Public Service Commission for the people who would be sorting the mail with automatic machines? They set it at 50 cents an hour less than for people sorting mail manually. I am not a expert on job classification, but one would have to be an idiot not to accept the fact that a person watching letters spewed through the machine at the rate of thousands a minute must concentrate a lot more than a person working at it manually.
That is what the Public Service Commission and the Post Office Department wanted to impose unilaterally on the employees. The employees had to threaten a work stoppage before the Post Office Department and the government relented.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question?

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext: Yes, if it is not taken off my time.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext: I am sure the hon. member would not want to use the word threaten. There was a work stoppage, I think the hon. member made that point, but perhaps he would want to explain what happened as a result of the strike.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will be very happy to debate all these questions with the Postmaster General at the time when the estimates are brought before us and both he and I have time. The Minister said the government has gone as far as it can and that there is no more money. One would think that the offer which the government has made was made at the beginning of the negotiations. The fact is that there was little meaningful negotiation until the workers took a strike vote.
The minister suggests that they took the strike vote surreptitiously and that they went on strike surreptitiously. The fact is that they went on strike when the minister instructed his officials that there would have to be a settlement in an hour or there would be nothing to talk about. If anybody precipitated the strike it was the minister. What happened in the days after the strike? In the first few days after the strike they settled 128 clauses which were in dispute. Why did they not settle them before they went on strike? The minister said that they settled the question of casual workers. Of course they did. When? Either just before the workers went on strike or just after.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I never mentioned casuals. I apologize if the hon. member misunderstood me. I said we settled the issue of automation before they want on strike, and I said we did not settle the 128 clauses the day after they went on strike.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext:
What I am saying is that a substantial part of what had been agreed to when the strike started or just after it started was agreed to not in the months when they were negotiating with a fair amount of good will but only with the threat of a strike, or after the strike started. We can talk about this when we have time. I say that the question of casual labour was not settled until very close to the time, either just before of just after the strike started. I say that the question of shift premiums was not settled until that time. I say that the question of premiums for part-time employees on weekends was not settled until that time.
What I am saying is that if the Post Office Department had been generous and fair, and if it had indicated it wanted to reach a settlement on some of those issues which go back more than ten years, and if the union leaders are everything that the minister says they are and everything that the hon. member for York East (Mr. Collenette) says they are-I do not know, I am not involved in the negotiations and I am not a member of the union-then I have enough faith in the common sense and good judgment of the oridnary worker to know that they would oust the leaders who are not doing a job for them, and elect others. But that is their business and they will handle it in a democratic way. They do not need me and they do not need the minister to tell them how to run their business.
Let me conclude by saying-I think the minister was not here when I said it at the beginning-that it is obvious to me that the minister's position has hardened to such a point that there can be no settlement with this minister because what he is saying to the workers-I am not discussing at the moment the merits or demerits of their case-in that he represents the Government of Canada which has given these workers everything they can get, and that if they want to stay out six months, they can do so, but they will not get any more. I say that this is not bargaining in good faith.
The minister may feel badly, he may be insulted, but I say he is anti-labour, he is as stubborn and mean as the management of the aircraft plant in Longueuil which kept its workers out for months, or was it years? I think the minister is trying to be fair, and he honestly believes that he is a friend of labour, I say to him-not that he is 100 per cent right, or that the union is 100 percent right-that he has become so emotionally involved in this question that he can no longer look at it objectively or rationally. He outht to remove himself voluntarily from the negotiations at this point. That is why we suggest that with the agreement of both sides a mediator should be appointed to look at the whole question and report back to both parties.
Maybe a mediator would say that the government has given everything it has to give, but both sides could make a fresh start on this strike. The minister says it is not causing great hardship, but it is. It is causing difficulties and trouble for thousands of ordinary people in Canada. Maybe after that action has been taken the strike could be brought to a conclusion with justness and fairness to both sides.

Mr. Speaker, in the short time that I have been here I think most
November 17, 1975

members of this House have come to realize that I am a very conciliatory person, a very reasonable person. I suppose most members know that I am from a constituency where most voters are union members. But I also happen to be in a rather unusual situation of not only having a very strong labour representation but I am one of those people to whom the two previous speakers kept referring, a small businessman. I rather basked in the warmth of their concern for the small businessman because I realized that I am one of the few in this House.

speechtext: Bryce doesn't worry about it.

I had a nagging doubt about whether it was the small businessman they were concerned about. As one involved with accounts receivable which are normally sent through the mail, and upon which I depend for my survival in business every month, I have found alternate ways of receiving the funds. We no longer mail them out; we use the phone, an invention which has been around for quite a while. We telephone people whose accounts are receivable and ask them to come to the office instead of sending cash by mail. People do pay their bills when informed of the amount, and most small businessmen have phones-at least in British Columbia.
It seemed to be indicated that a high cost was involved with the use of the telephone and courier services, but it is very interesting to note that the Insurance Corporation of British Columbia, which is a government run institution, is providing an excellent service. We pick up our mail from their claims office and, not only that, but they are willing to pick up all the mail for the other independent companies and provide that service. So, Mr. Speaker, business people are perhaps being used as a political ploy to bring into this House the issue of the postal service, in order to have it said that we cannot exist without it.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext: Be serious.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext: I am being very serious.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext: You are not.

speechtext:
Most small businessmen would agree to a fair and just settlement-they would put that before an immediate profit for a few months or a few weeks. Most small businessmen are responsible-I wish some other people were as responsible.
We have had the occasional strike in British Columbia. Unions such as the IWA have been known to strike, but I cannot recall an occasion when the IWA did not inform their membership of the packet that was being presented by management. I have sometimes had doubts as to when strikes should be called and people go out on strike because, from a humanitarian point of view, the wage earner is the one who ultimately suffers.
Although I can appreciate the concern that was expressed by several other members for the public and for business, may I say in all honesty that the person who suffers most is the worker on strike. He cannot afford to lose wages because he is not one of the high wage earners in our economy.
Postal Strike

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext: What are you suggesting-that we do away with strikes?

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext:
There are several other reasons why I believe the strike was unnecessary. First of all, the mediation report was accepted by the government and, second, the same contract that was offered to the inside workers had been accepted by the outside workers.
I think it is fair to say that historically the two unions have run in tandem. Those who suggest that the inside workers should receive more than the outside workers would only sow seeds of discontent for the future. The IWA and the CPU in British Columbia generally get exactly the same wage settlement because of the type of work they do. Anyone who suggests we should start bringing imbalance in there would be sowing the seeds of discontent for future negotiations.
Third, Mr. Speaker, on October 13 the government brought in guidelines. The union must surely realize that to stay out for six weeks, two months, or whatever period, would be fruitless unless we as a government decided we would not abide by our own guidelines-that we would scrap the program and go into some sort of anarchy. It is the responsibility of the minister in this first test of how we consider the guidelines to make sure that they are followed.
There is the mediation report, parity with the outside workers, and the guidelines. To go on strike and not refer back to their membership is irresponsible leadership, and is not the fault of the inside workers.
As I said earlier, the strike was unnecessary and simply weakens the bargaining position. The government cannot lock out a union. There was no necessity for the strike, and every union member on strike is losing approximately $40 or $50 per day.
There are going to be no winners, Mr. Speaker. Business will not win, the strikers will not win, the people of Canada who depend upon the mail service will not win. Everybody is a loser, but the biggest losers are the strikers. Regardless of any final settlement, they are going to lose money. I wish more members would think about them rather than the people who might not be able to write to an aunt in Regina. That is an inconvenience, but it is not something we cannot live without. The strikers are not highly paid and they can ill afford to lose money. That is a tragedy in a fruitless, unreasonable, and stupid strike.
So far the average inside postal worker has lost $1,000. In order to gain 20 cents an hour they would have to work
5,000	hours. I do not think the minister is anti-labour any more than I am. I am concerned about the workers, not the negotiators who, like most negotiators, can take care of themselves. Mostly I am concerned about the sorters who do the work.
The minister has fought hard to include the automation clause in the negotiations. He has done an excellent job, considering the existence of the guidelines, the settlement of the outside workers, and the matter of the arbitration hearing.

November 17, 1975
Postal Strike
Hon. members, I think, are not concerned about the Post Office workers' right to strike. They want to see inside workers presented with the facts of a settlement. If they do not like the settlement they can refuse it; no one says they should not refuse it if they so choose. Many postal workers, especially in my area, do not know what the package contains. That package should be made known to them for study, and acceptance or rejection.
I have been in touch with many Canadians; their message is loud and clear: if the government is serious about fighting inflation, do not give in to blackmail; do not be coerced, because the people of Canada can put up for some time with not getting mail. The people do not expect the government to give in to unreasonable demands.
I hope that those who are losing money can vote on these questions. We live in a democratic society. Surely the workers in the union should decide their own destiny. After all they are losing money and they should have a voice in accepting or rejecting the settlement. I think the government can live either with an acceptance or rejection. The workers must be free to decide. I therefore hope that the minister will find some way of ensuring that they can decide their own destiny.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government should have initiated this debate a couple of weeks ago to obtain a consensus of the House, as most of us are fed up to the teeth with the utter nonsense involving the Post Office. Now that we are debating the issue I hope the Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey) will stop straddling the fence and take steps immediately to get the mail moving.
I know that the government does not want to do anything to help the bandits in the postal unions save face, and I know that the two birds who are holding up the works would like nothing better than have us order the postal workers back to the job. Then they could say that they were only trying to get the posties a better deal but the government would not go back to the table. No matter what we do to get the mails moving again, those two birds, the squeaking, howling parrot, and that Scotch buzzard, Davidson, should be sent packing. Both are no better than blackmailers, and I know that the majority of Canadians are as fed up as I am with this kind of blackmail.
I was really surprised when the great champion of the working man, the leader of the NDP, earlier refused unanimous consent for our motion under Standing Order 43 which called for a national referendum, by secret ballot, on the government's final wage offer. The leader of the NDP must surely know that there is a division in the ranks of the CUPW and that the only democratic way it can be resolved is by a secret ballot vote. Perhaps the hon. member's sentiments are with the union chiefs, not with the workers. It could be that, like Joe Davidson, he is afraid to allow the workers to vote in a supervised, secret ballot referendum.
This afternoon I was speaking to the radio station of my area and was told that in southern Ontario the following post offices are now open; Alliston, Borden, Aurora, Huntsville, Keswick, Midland, Orillia, Penetang and Bradford. This represents 56 per cent of the workers of the area, but does not include Toronto.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext: Don't forget Elmira and Orangeville.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext: Yes. As I say, that does not include that postal monstrosity on Front Street, Toronto.

speechtext: I didn't know you had bought real estate.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext:
I have not. I talked to the radio station in my riding. There happens to be one in Parry Sound-Muskoka.
It is high time the Postmaster General put aside his fears that he might offend someone if he orders the postal workers back to their jobs. It is time for the Postmaster General to stop worrying about whether or not he will help Davidson and Parrot save face. It is time for the minister to save the postal service; then we can take any other steps necessary to prevent this sort of thing happening every couple of months.
The minister has been saying that the mail may not move again until Easter. Although this may be true if we sit by and do nothing, I think we have given the union chiefs time enough to resolve this matter if they really have it in their mind to settle the strike. It is obvious from all the grandstanding that Davidson and Parrot have been doing that they do not have any intention of acting responsibly. They seem to be basking in the attention they are getting from the media, and when I see them prancing and preening on television I cannot see that they have anything on their minds except themselves.
Some NDP spokesmen have said that the Postmaster General has behaved like a prima donna on television. Certainly he has appeared on TV, but he does not take a back seat to Parrot. I have watched Parrot for some time, and the only time his mouth did not move was for the three or four hours he sat in this gallery with his henchmen listening to the debate. Now I see that he has vanished, like the Arabs.

speechtext: Should that not be henchwoman?

Let's call them hench people.
It is a matter of record that my party has done just as much to further the cause of collective bargaining as those so-called champions of the little people over on my left. It seems ironic to them, I would think, that those solid citizens they are so pleased to call the little people, trimmed the sails of the NDP in the last election.

speechtext: Not in the Ontario election.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext:
The working people are pretty big people and it begins to look as though the wallop they pack in the polling booth is giving the NDP a sore jaw. The next time the NDP leader refuses to allow a simple motion an Standing Order 43 to pass, to give those people a chance to vote on whether they want to work, perhaps his own supporters should take him behind the woodshed for a little heart to heart talk.
I have always defended the right of workers to bargain and have a direct hand in deciding their wages and working conditions. This extends to the right to strike when their employers will not bargain in good faith, and to any
|Mr. Anderson.)
November 17, 1975

other reasonable grievance. However, the inside postal workers have been offered a reasonable wage increase. They have also received other concessions from the government. We have come to the point now where we have to decide on just whom we want to run the Post Office, the unions or the Postmaster General. I think the choice is obvious. After all, collective bargaining means just that. It does not mean that the unions demand and the government gives.
If we have reached the point where any union, whichever one it is, will not accept any less than it demands and will withdraw its services until all its demands are met, we have already exhausted the collective bargaining process. It is not bargaining any longer, it is blackmail; and I will not sit still and allow anyone to blackmail me or my constituents.
I think that the time has arrived when we should take a close look at where we are with respect to the matter of collective bargaining and the right to strike, especially in the area of essential services. After all, we have come a long way from the days of the sweat shop, the 14-hour work day, and the rest of the horrors of the early years of the industrial revolution. We have grown up, and in most cases it must be agreed that management and labour have grown up together.
We have labour legislation on the books concerning almost every aspect of the labour market. We have laws governing safety measures on the job and other working conditions, laws governing minimum wages and laws that compel management to deal fairly with labour in disputes. It is time to decide just how much protection we should legislate for the forgotten Canadian, the innocent victims of strikes when essential services are withdrawn by arrogant and thoughtless union bosses who feel that they can get everything they want by denying the public their services.
We have to devise some system of mediation or arbitration whereby workers in essential services are given every light to bargain, but where they are not given the right to strike, or threaten to strike, in order to force a settlement. At the present time, for instance, aside from the fact that Canadians are not able to write or receive letters from friends and loved ones, the entire national economy is being adversely affected by the postal strike, a strike by ' the way that should not have been called in the first place.
Businesses are suffering through not being able to send bills or receive payments for goods and services supplied. Some businesses have already failed, and others are having a tough time trying to wait out this latest postal strike.
I have not kept score on the work stoppages, slowdowns, strikes, and other interruptions of the postal service in the past ten years, but I have heard other people estimate that these things occur every five or six months. Even if it were only once every year, or every two years, it would be too often. We have stumbled along now for several years with a postal service that is not only slow and in other ways
Postal Strike
inefficient, but is completely inoperable every few months. I say to this House that we must make a decision, and we must make it soon.
Either we are going to continue to fund a postal service that is so inefficient that it is the laughing stock of the western world, a postal service run by a handful of union bandits instead of by the Postmaster General, or we are going to decide to take a new direction. Our Post Office has gone down about as low as it can go; in fact it is at a standstill. And that seems to be the accepted posture of the Canadian Post Office. Now I believe that it is time for us to start looking up. We have an opportunity to take matters as they stand now and work out a plan as to what we want in the way of a postal service in Canada. If we decide what we want, we can get it.
Since the present strike started I have been forced to send my weekly newspaper reports to my constituency by bus. The cost of doing this is a great deal more than if I had access to the federal postal system, but a package sent from my office on Thursday evening arrives at my constituency office the following day. That is service, the kind of service we could and should get from our Post Office, but it has been many a year since we have had that kind of service from our Post Office.
I am afraid that we are past the point where we can reasonably expect to get first class mail service again, at least not in the foreseeable future. The only way we will ever have an efficient mail service, one that does not shut down every time there is a minor dispute between the unions and the Postmaster General, is for this House to give the minister a mandate to clean house in the Post Office and establish once and for all that the Postmaster General is in charge of the Post Office. Anyone who does not want to accept that simple fact should be told to seek employment elsewhere. Right now the postal employees are turning up their noses at a wage increase that will bring their annual income to above $13,000 per year and, believe me, I challenge each and every one of the people who sneer at that salary to try to find a job anywhere else that will pay that kind of money for doing what they do in the Post Office.
Joe Davidson has a lot of his members believing that he can get them that kind of money for working only 30 hours a week if they will just hold out and refuse to sort mail until the government gives in. I think that the temper of this House is about the same as the temper of the Canadian people at this point. The majority of us are fed up with Davidson's and Parrot's posturing and primping. It is past time for us to serve notice on them that their tactics are not going to work any more, not for another day or for another hour.
They have shown us that they are not interested in anyone else except themselves. Davidson has said on public television "to hell with the public". Only a few days ago he laughed and said that he guessed that he would have to live with that remark. You bet he will have to live with it. I say to Davidson, "to hell with power-hungry, irresponsible and arrogant union leaders." Perhaps "holy Joe" believes that he can bring Canada to its knees and that he can keep sticking the knife in and twisting it until he gets everything he wants. The trouble is that even if he gets everything he demands today, he will be back next

I think we should take this opportunity tonight to let the Postmaster General know that the vast majority of people favour his stand not to give in to Joe Davidson's blackmail tactics. I would like to be able to say that the Postmaster General has my unqualified support, but to get that he is going to have to do more than just stand pat. The minister accepted the Post Office portfolio, and the portfolio carries with it a responsibility to maintain postal service in Canada.
Standing up to Davidson's bombastic posturing is a good start, but it is only a start. To get the show back on the road the minister must take the necessary steps to see that the rank and file of the CUPW are allowed to vote in a national, secret-ballot referendum, under proper supervision to ensure that the union executive is not able to rig the election. At this point in time I do not have one iota of faith in Mr. Davidson's integrity. I think that it is very important to allow the union members to vote without fear of retaliation from the thugs in the union.
I heard on tonight's radio news that people have been threatened in different parts of the country and have had threats made against their families. That is not the way decent people conduct business. That is the way gangsters and thugs do business, and it appears that that is the way Joe Davidson would prefer to do business.
In conclusion I would like to call on all of my colleagues, on this side of the House and on the government benches, to let the Postmaster General know that we have had enough of the nonsense that has paralyzed the Post Office and that we will support him in any positive steps he chooses to take to restore postal service in Canada. I do not hesitate to remind the minister that there are hundreds of thousands of people looking for jobs in Canada. If the people in the Post Office do not want to work, then fire them and hire people who want to work.
Let us stop playing games and let us keep in mind that the Post Office belongs to the Canadian people and that it is an essential service. To the Postmaster General I say: let us get the show back on the road.

Madam Speaker, my remarks this evening will be very brief. The subject of debate tonight is of great importance to the nation, all sections of which are at the mercy of certain hardened attitudes and certain individuals.
The long term effects of the continued breakdown of collective bargaining will cause substantial damage not only to those directly involved but to the economy generally; indeed, the effect might be to drag the nation to the ground.
I have a great deal of respect for the Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey) mainly because at one time he happened to live in the constituency of Moncton. But the remarks of the Postmaster General tonight have done nothing but add further fuel to an inferno which is already spreading great damage and causing irreparable harm. Likewise the union representatives have in the past done and said things which should have been left undone and unsaid. Communication via the news media is no way to carry on collective bargaining.
The nation needs a postal service, and the provision of a postal service is a responsibility of government and of parliament. Most nations pride themselves on their postal services. It is time we put our postal service in place. This affects not only business but every home and every individual. The postal strike has gone on long enough now, and we can no longer allow our citizens to suffer because of the personal attitudes of the individuals concerned. There is still a chance for collective bargaining, and if both parties are still concerned about the public interest, then whether through the appointment of a mediator, or by an immediate return to work voluntarily, or by legislation parliament should concentrate, by every means possible, on getting the postal services back into operation.
This is no time to rehash history. We must look to the future, the future of the postal service, the future of our industry and commerce, the future of our people. We must put a stop to the damage and inconvenience which the public is experiencing. We have a responsibility; we must accept it, and take positive steps. We have a job to do, let us get on with that job. There has been a great deal of misunderstanding on the part of both parties. We should attempt to resolve the problem once and for all. If the Postmaster General does not intend to bring in back-to-work legislation immediately, then I would suggest, if he and his colleagues are agreeable, and if the union repre-

sentatives are agreeable, that as an independent member of parliament I would be willing to sit down with both parties, not in Ottawa, but in a faraway, neutral, friendly territory, namely, Moncton, New Brunswick, in a sincere effort to help resolve the postal strike forthwith.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to join all those who have spoken on the motion before us and depending on one's point of view in the debate, we all seem to be a little right since, the situation being what it is, we must confess that unfortunately once more it proves to be disastrous and shows beyond any doubt that we are not yet mature enough to find appropriate ways of preventing it from happening.
I should like to take some time to deal with that particular angle, so that we can realize once and for all the need to discover normal ways of arriving at settlements agreeable to parties concerned, not only in the Post Office, but also in all sectors of economic activity in the country, thinking precisely that that strike will end one day and we will immediately embark on another one somewhere else.
That is the most deceiving and unjustifiable thing, Madam Speaker. How come indeed, in 1975, we are still obliged to resort to extreme action to solve problems? That is not good enough. We are not living in the Middle Ages. Communications today have developed so much that, as I said, it is unacceptable that an agreement cannot be reached, that it is impossible to talk, discuss and reach a decision. That is not good enough! And moreover, we find that those means which should be used in the last resort are in current use. They are now commonplace, as it were. We live with that. We accept the fact, we admit it and are ready to go on like this.
This is so true, Madam Speaker, that after the first indications that a strike was possible and could last a certain time, already arrangements were being made to . cope with this strike and try to deliver the mail just the same, to settle the most urgent problems, such as the delivery of old age pensions, family allowances and unemployment insurance benefits. I found it quite strange that steps were being taken even before the strike. This means
|Mr. Condon.]
that we find quite normal to resort to a contingency plan which should only be considered in an extreme situation.
Madam Speaker, it is very sad indeed to find that we have reached such a point. I would not want to decide who is right and who is wrong, but rather I wonder whether the time has not come to seriously consider ways to settle the major problems that strikes have become. Why not once and for all stop to think and find mechanisms which would make strikes useless? I would not say that the right to strike should be taken away, but I say that we are irresponsible if in 1975 we fail to find a way to prevent strikes.
Of course, as others have stressed before me, very often workers resort to this extreme method, the strike, to win their case, but that does not always reflect the views of the workers as a whole in a given area. I agree with those who advocate a secret vote and not a vote by a show of hands, so that every worker may be allowed to voice his real opinion, namely, whether he wants to resort to strike or not. It is quite obvious that, unfortunately, many union leaders seem to want to justify their role and their job. To acknowledge that fact is not being anti-labour. Unfortunately, such are the facts.
It seems therefore that these union leaders or important labour associates justify their positions. In order to prove to the rank and file that they are necessary, useful and essential, they cause or provoke troubles artificially, for, as indicated by one of the previous speakers, it is something of a paradox that while there are hundreds of thousands of workers who are anxiously seeking employment, others are not satisfied with the jobs they have. Quite a paradox!
I feel it is necessary, however, to take into account the situations as they are, and to find accordingly a solution to the present conflict, but especially, as I stated in my opening remarks, devote some time seriously considering final solutions to all the conflicts which are troubling the Canadian economy, concerning society and demoralizing our people. Let us not deny it: we have reached that stage.
Madam Speaker, the Postmaster General, the government and this Parliament must absolutely decide to put an end to that postal strike and, overmore, to find a way to avoid strikes once and for all. As I suggested through a motion under Standing Order 43, when we have found a way to avoid that strike, it will have become obsolete.
It has often been suggested, and I say it again, that we will finally have to set up labour courts, similar to our courts of justice. Those who would be called upon to judge will, of course, be chosen very objectively. They would have the same authority as ordinary courts. That is the solution towards which we must strive, which we must achieve so that, when there is disagreement between employer and employee, after discussions have been held, if no agreement has been reached then both parties can go before one of those labour tribunals who will pass objective judgment on the worthiness of the claims of the employee and the value of the objections of the employee. The judgment once passed, would then be irrevocable just as that of our courts of justice.
Madam Speaker, these abnormal situations must be done away with; I would even call them childish. I have four little boys, the oldest is 13, the youngest six; they say at
November 17, 1975

home: If you do not give me this, I shall do that. This is childish.
We are adults and we are discussing simply to get to blackmail: give me this or else I stop working, give us that or we do not distribute mail any more. It is terrible to have to resort to such procedures in 1975. It is childish.
It is absolutely necessary to find a solution to ensure that these things do not happen and this is why I do insist on a basic agreement, a major settlement for all conflicts which are likely to happen; this way, it would not be necessary to discuss repeatedly a settlement in a given area.
I think that this should be taken into account and that we should move towards an immediate review in this field. True, others have talked about it before me. To whom are those strikes most harmful? The first ones to bear the brunt are the strikers themselves.
It is unfortunate that this should be so. They are those who will be the first victims. Evidently the whole society will also suffer the consequences of their action, but I believe that as representatives of the people we cannot let this go on unchecked for long.
Therefore, in my view, the minister and the government are under obligation to settle this conflict immediately with whatever means are at our disposal. But we should also endeavour to find real solutions to those problems so that they never come up to the House again.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am certainly surprised that a member of this House, especially the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Anderson) who spoke recently could be so narrow minded that he would think everyone in this country could use the telephone and would not need mail service. I am surprised at the intelligence of such a member of this House.
I have a story to tell. I want every member of this House to picture a small, remote, northern settlement which has no television, no newspapers, and depends on airstrips and the mail as its means of communication with the outside world. The story I have to bring to the attention of this House is not fiction. It is an indication of how some people try to cope with government bungling. In November of 1974 a little old lady in a remote area of Manitoba was visited by her doctor who prescribed medication for the treatment of her ailment. The nearest drug store was some 236 air miles away. This lady is a senior citizen. She is dependent on her pension. Her pension is her only means of support.
She had the problem of making arrangements with the drug store some 236 air miles away to send in her medication by mail each month on the same plane that brought in her pension cheque. The arrangements were completed and everything went well until the postal strike of last February. At that time, as we all know, the mail came to a complete stop. This really hurts the people in remote areas because the mail is their only means of communication with the outside world.
This little old lady was not going to be caught without her medication. She scurried around and made arrange-
Postal Strike
ments to have her medication brought in on the sched-runs which are part of the class III operations of the air carriers in the north. These are weekly runs into the various communities. Everything was arranged. She was to have a parcel shipped in a little package. It would come in on the sched-run. In this way she would receive her medication. Thankfully the strike was settled without too much delay and she was able to have her pension cheque to pay for the medication.
But this little old lady did not intend to be caught without her medication again, so she continued to receive the medication in the little package on the sched-run. She did not intend to depend on the Post Office to bring this much needed medication to her. This practice worked fine until, lo and behold, the Ministry of Transport in July made a decision. There are five airstrips in northern Manitoba that are served exclusively by air. These communities found that their airstrips were taken out of the class III operations and they were virtually left with an air system by which there would be only charter aircraft coming into their area.
The residents of northern Manitoba wondered just who would make a decision like this to cut off not only their mail but their only means of transportation. They came to the decision that the person responsible was probably some bureaucrat sitting in a comfortable office in Ottawa who had an all-year round airstrip at his service, and who was not thinking of the people in the remote areas.
Now, back to the story. After the bureaucratic ruling was made that these airstrips were not up to the national standard necessary for air carriers to operate a class III service, the operation was suspended except for charter flights. This was the second blow to strike this little old lady, but she was determined to live and cope with the decision of this great government. She made arrangements with the pilot to bring in the medication on the same day the pension cheque arrived. At last she could rest; but not for long, because, lo and behold, by the middle of October another postal strike was under way.
This little old lady was not going to give up. She had ten months of fighting with the government. She tried to outsmart the government. She was bound she would fight with the government to obtain the medication she so desperately needed. The medication had helped her regain strength so she walked down to the local post office which had remained opened. Although the post office was open it was only handling local mail. After she had arrived at the post office she spoke with the local postmaster who really did not have much to do because there was not much mail to handle. The mail was not coming in from the outside to this remote area.
After jawing for a while with the postmaster she asked if he had anything that she might read. Time was very heavy on her hands now. He said "Yes, we have some material here. On the last plane that came in before the strike we received 700 copies of the government's latest shiny new edition of 'How the Tax Dollar is Spent' ".
The citizens of Canada have no one to bargain on their behalf. This lady has no one to bargain on her behalf. She is caught in the middle. She does not belong to a union and therefore has no one to fight for her. She has no communication with the outside world. She depends entirely on the

November 17, 1975
Postal Strike
mail service to bring her news of the outside world and the medication she so desperately needs. I cite only this example. This situation could be duplicated many times if we think of the parts of Canada other than the great corridor running from Montreal to Windsor.
There is another part of the country in which people are suffering because of the mail strike. I say, let us get the mail moving again. Then we should start working on Canada's postal service in an effort to bring it back to the excellent high standard of efficiency it once had. In my estimation at one time Canada had one of the best postal services in the world. I would certainly support the Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey) in his efforts to get the Post Office back on the right road because it is Canada and the people who live in this country who suffer.

speechtext:
I said not necessarily in here. Then I have heard other suggestions, particularly from the NDP, which would give away the public purse completely. I think that between these areas there is something worthwhile to be said.
The problems of the Post Office today are not something that just happened in the last three or four weeks. They are very long term problems which go back to the early 1960s and the relationship between employees and employers and between the management and some of the local post offices and their employees. Sometimes this situation has been described as open warfare.
The Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey) is perhaps the one person who is most aware of that. I talked to him many times before he was given this post and I know he understands these problems. We are talking about relations that in many cases are really deplorable. When he came to this job, and I talked to him about it at that time, his ambition was to get a good settlement for the postal employees and give them a feeling that they are somebody, that they are important, and to develop relations in the Post Office

which would result in a decent postal service, the kind we had in the early 1960's and before. That was his aim then, and that is his aim today. So what did he do? He sat down with the Treasury Board, he sat down with the Letter Carriers Union of Canada, and he got a good settlement, far more than the Treasury Board wanted to pay.
This settlement with the letter carriers was ratified by 82 per cent of the employees, and they are a satisfied group.
Now we sit down with the other group, the CUPW. This is a group that has perhaps more problems. They do a job that many people do not want to do, it is a repetitive job, there are conflicts inside. The outside workers can get out more and when they finish their day, they can leave their work. These postal employees are good people, good, solid Canadians, the backbone of our country. They are not wild radicals, but they have problems. So what did we do? We talked to them about all kinds of problems. One of them is the fear of automation. They were concerned about automation and about their jobs and their stake in the community. This is an important concern. We talked about those concerns.
I can tell you there are all kinds of other areas in this country where that has not been the way things have gone. We have said that we would protect these peoples' jobs. We talked about casuals. We were not just talking about what to do when an extra employee comes in, but we talked about that letter sorter who knows 1,500 routes and streets and where the letters went. We talked about that skilled man. When we said we would keep casuals down to a minimum we were saying that that particular full time employee is an important person, and we will pay him time and a half before we bring in a casual because he is important, he has valuable skills, and he can produce for us.
These are the kinds of things that have gone into this settlement, the kind of things that this minister and I want to see happen. We want to see a better postal service. We know that if you give these people a better chance, they will produce, because this is what everyone does. I say to you that that is the kind of settlement we wanted. There are limits, and the limit clearly is the amount that was given to the LCUC. This limit was the 38 per cent monetary settlement. For all kinds of reasons this is the limit, and the only reason we can get this through the Anti-Inflation Board is because historically there is a relationship between the letter carriers and the inside workers.
What concerns me tonight is the suggestion I hear from the NDP that we must have more mediation. To me mediation means one thing, it means getting someone who will find a middle ground between the union and the management. In this particular area there is no middle ground, and 38 per cent is the limit.
The second thing I heard from the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) was that he would like to see the postal workers' day cut from 40 to 35 hours. That is a very desirable thing, but when you suggest that you will take a 38 per cent increase and then you compound that by a 12 per cent increase, you end up with about 52 per cent. That is far more than the Treasury will bear, far more than the guidelines will allow, and in general it is not acceptable. These are the suggestions I have heard this evening.
November 17, 1975

I have heard others say that we should legislate the postal workers back to work. I think that today in this country there is a lot of support for the Postmaster General. He has suggested that in the next 24 hours he will put the content of the Moisan report to the people of this country and to the employees of the Post Office. He is saying that the content of this report has been basically accepted in the collective bargaining. It is the hope of the government, of the minister and of myself, that the employees will look at this, see that it is fair and, with the power they have within their union, will go back to work.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it has been suggested that one's life is somehow enriched by every new experience through which one passes, but I have been wondering just how my life has been enriched by the new experience I am having tonight, because never in my life have I endeavoured to preach a sermon or make a speech at half past one in the morning. I prefer a different time in the day for it in ordinary circumstances. But I do rise tonight to add my voice to the call for immediate and decisive action to bring to an end a strike in the postal service that has seriously affected and is seriously affecting the whole country.
It is not my intention to deal with the circumstances leading up to this stoppage in postal services, nor will I attempt to attach blame for the situation in which we presently find ourselves. I think sufficient has been said tonight to indicate that it has been of long duration, it has been stormy, and it has not resulted in satisfactory solutions to the problem. We are still in the position where the country is deprived of what we ordinarily consider to be a service that is vitally important to the nation.
I should like to say that the time has come, and actually is overdue, when the public interest must be taken into account and something tangible done to assist them. No doubt there are legitimate grievances behind the postal workers' decision to strike. No matter what the suggestion of leadership, I cannot imagine a group of responsible people putting the country to the inconvenience and hardship of a strike if there was no ground whatsoever for discontent and unrest.
Listening to the discussions that have taken place and the questions asked in this House and answered by the Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey), it seems to me that the government has not been sufficiently sensitive to the causes of concern, frustration and desperation that these workers have experienced.
As we consider the national interest tonight I would say the time for decisive action has come to get the postal service functioning again, and to remove inconvenience and hardship from the Canadian people who have not contributed to the situation.
What we are having tonight is perhaps the continuation of a debate carried on over the past several weeks. The question has been asked; is the postal service an essential service? Without getting too deeply involved in that aspect I would say there is a relationship between that issue and the reason why the strike should be settled forthwith. To the people of Canada who have some degree of social
Postal Strike
mobility and a measure of economic freedom, the Post Office might not be essential. To large corporations which have ways and means to circumvent the Post Office, again the institution may not be essential.
I might say here, however, that there are many Canadians with whom I come in contact who are not getting along fairly well without regular mail delivery. I was amazed to hear some hon. members speaking tonight and playing down the serious effect the strike is having on certain sectors of the economy. Millions of Canadians and thousands of small businesses look upon the mail service as an essential service, and they are facing real difficulty these days.
We have been assured that provision has been made to get social security and other pension cheques into the hands of those who require them, but that may not be as easy as is pictured. There is the prospect of some people not getting their cheques for some time and many of them are dependent on the cheques coming right on the dot. If they do not they will have difficulty surviving for a week or two. I think the postal service is absolutely necessary to those people.
Hundreds of small businesses, in my constituency and all across the country, are experiencing problems in collecting accounts and sending out invoices and so on. I was amazed to hear a member from British Columbia, who is a small businessman, say that he was getting along very well thank you. He played down the difficulties facing small businesses. Perhaps I have been speaking to smaller businessmen than he, but they say they are facing real problems. We had better not play it down. These sectors of our economy view a dependable mail service as an essential service. Most of them are not big enough to hire their own courier service, or get around the Post Office by some other means.
Numbers of non-profit organizations in this country provide humanitarian services for thousands of people and they depend on regular donations to keep functioning. They face difficulty now, however, and as a result many people are going to suffer because these humanitarian enterprises cannot carry on. That aspect of the situation should be considered.
Another aspect that warrants consideration is the undemocratic nature and dictatorial attitude of some of the union leaders in the strike. Right from the beginning the union leaders have been unwilling to submit the government's proposal to the membership for a vote. The reason is that they know the members do not want a continuation of the strike and would probably ratify the government's offer if it were submitted to a vote.
I understand that violence has been precipitated by union people at various areas across the country. In Ottawa last week an inside postal worker went on radio station CKOY to plead for support for a return to work and to clarify the government contract to his co-workers. I am told his life was threatened by the union on the open line show.
In my riding individuals who returned to work were harassed and theatened by a group who came from Vancouver. They were presumably sent on union orders to intimidate those who had returned to work. This type of

November 17, 1975
Postal Strike
conduct, if advocated by the union, amounts to an antidemocratic and dictatorial attitude. As members of the House of Commons and on behalf of the citizens of the country, we should reject outright this type of activity.
I have a telegram here and I did call the officials concerned to ask if I could read it into the record. They told me to go ahead, but still I hesitate to do so. I would not like to think that reading it into the record would bring harassment, threats, and intimidation upon them. The gist of the message is lack of responsible leadership on both sides. A request has been made for the government to legislate the union membership back to work. There is some indication of a wish to have the outstanding issues submitted to binding arbitration. That is the message coming to us from a local postal union and it indicates the attitude of many postal workers.
The Postmaster General should be commended for saying in the House that workers suspended by the union can still work in the Post Office. The statement will help to alleviate the fears of some postal workers. A union official indicated to me that workers have been threatened with the withdrawal of union cards, with the take-over by head office of their union, and with loss of jobs, pensions, and other benefits accruing to them from years of service in the Post Office.
I support something definite being done to bring this matter to a satisfactory conclusion, because the sorts of threats to which I referred cannot be reconciled with the union's professed concern for the welfare of Post Office employees for that attitude, if it exists, is more reprehensible than injustice from which workers may have suffered.
The Postmaster General is not without blame, as his comments have generated resentment instead of good will. He has failed to act decisively in resolving the longest postal strike in our history.
All this points to one thing, the necessity for negotiating and concluding negotiations before the expiry of the contracts. Why should the parties wait until a contract has expired and then go through the motions of negotiation, conciliation, or whatever may take place? I think these matters ought to be considered before the present contract expires; and the process can be carried on by negotiation and mutual agreement between the two groups concerned. Perhaps it ought to be brought to final arbitration and a settlement imposed in the interest of the national economy.
I appreciate the opportunity for placing my views on record at this early hour of the morning and trust that action will be taken to resolve the strike, return the workers to their jobs, and reinstate our postal service.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me say with all the strength of my feelings that I am proud to associate myself with the Postmaster General's actions thus far. Probably I shall be proud of his actions in future. We are dealing with an existing situation, not with a situation which may exist in the future. For that reason we must be careful to consider the best way of dealing
(Mr. Patterson.]
with this matter in the present in order that we do not adversely affect events in the future.
His past actions show the Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey) to be a most human and interested person. He has been worried about what might happen to workers with the advent of automation. His concern was apparent when the huge plant at Mississauga was erected. He wondered if the workers' social adjustment had been taken into consideration, if their physical amenities like showers and recreational facilities were adequate, and if there was opportunity for them to socialize after work. In my presence, and on television, the Postmaster General has indicated his concern for Post Office workers, and I am confident that he, being a most human, warm Canadian, will do all he can for them.
I cannot forget what a great part the postman played in my growing up. The pension cheque was important in my household, my father being a totally disabled veteran. I remember the old postman sometimes coming to my mother and telling her not to worry, that he would speak to the sorters and bring the cheque as quickly as possible. Today, when so many people live in apartment buildings, postmen put the mail in mail boxes without ever talking to the people they serve. Yet the letter carrier can still show strong interest in those he serves. I think the Postmaster General understands all this.
Let me tell hon. members a story about the Postmaster General which he probably does not know I know. But, after all, little happens in Verdun that is not known fairly soon in places far away. Recently I was speaking at the anniversary of the church in the riding, and I learned that the Postmaster General was speaking that same evening in that city. All this took place before the present strike.
At that time we were witnessing a slowdown of the mails, and I understand that the Postmaster General was on the way home from his speaking engagement at about the present time of day, in the early hours of the morning. He turned to his driver and asked if anything of interest had happened in the constituency. He was told that a family in the constituency was expecting an important registered letter from Toronto; the family was anxiously awaiting it but it had not been delivered.
Apparently the Toronto office had clearly indicated that the letter had arrived at the old post office on Church Avenue, Verdun, but had not been sorted. The Postmaster General said, "Well, I guess we had better go down there." His driver said, "Is it not a little late? Should we not go home?" The Postmaster General said, "No" and went down to the post office.
You can just imagine the Postmaster General walking in the door of the post office in his tuxedo, and the surprise of the people behind the wicket. The Postmaster General asked about the letter, but was told that there had been so much mail that the letter probably had not been sorted. So the Postmaster General took off his evening jacket and said, "Let's look in that pile; perhaps we shall find it."
In the meantime the telephone rang. Apparently the manager in charge of the post office, realizing the urgency for the person concerned, had looked for the letter and delivered it by hand. So the Postmaster General put on his
November 17, 1975

coat, looked up and said. "If you ever need any help, give me a call and I will be glad to help you any time."
That shows you how human the Postmaster General is in his relations with the workers. He does not order, does not demand, but sets an example. He shows how the people should be served.
That is the kind of person I know the Postmaster General to be. I am not ashamed to speak this way, because when I was a young man at university and he was an alderman, he hired me to work for him. So I have had some strong experience of the man and that is why I have so much confidence in him.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext: Yes, and I have a tear in my eye.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext:
I am not interested in the hon. member's tears. I am interested in his listening, and in his saying something important, if he has anything important to say.
I have become convinced in the debate tonight. I have heard almost everyone stand up and say in a very sincere way what they think should be done. I did not get the impression that anyone stood up just for the sake of speaking. In my way I have spoken strongly to indicate that there are some people who have a close relationship with the Postmaster General and believe in him. That is my purpose in saying what I have said. Other members have stated ways in which they think the situation should be solved.
The major opposition has said, "Legislate them back to work to solve the situation." The NDP in its way has said, "Start bargaining all over again." The government, through the Postmaster General has said in very clear terms that we are on the beaches. That is what this is all about. This is what this war on avarice is all about.
We are on the beaches. We are speaking tonight as Canadians. Postmen, opposition, members of parliament, small businessmen, whatever your lot or your background may be, we are on the beaches. We do not feel embarrassed at standing there very firmly and saying we take the stand that the time for patriotism has come.
This is indeed a war of avarice. It must start at some point. We are fortunate that in our front echelon we have a Postmaster General who has taken that stand. That is the stand he has taken. If you listened to his speech you will note that he not so much wanted to tell you about the past but to do something now and, in doing something now, we might save the future.

which has become so serious in this country." I still have to conclude that because I am not getting through to the backbenchers.

If members opposite think that this is just a parliamentary discussion on whether or not we should legislate on a strike, we should not be speaking at this time of night. We are speaking on a very serious principle, whether the government at this moment is doing what it thinks is best for the good of this country and attempting to succeed in doing that without being delayed by many forces. The forces that will come after the Post Office will be many more. We are only facing one such night of debate.
I hope we will be standing here some night when I am hoarse, bedraggled, and worn, still saying one more chance. The Postmaster General is saying give those workers another chance to speak to their leaders. Let us give those leaders another chance to believe.

speechtext: They' are union leaders like I presume myself to be a leader in my constituency. They too are important. This the minister doesn't forget.
