subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate my colleague and friend, the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke), for moving the motion that is permitting us to have this special debate on the postal crisis this evening. Because it is already one o'clock in the morning I will try to be as brief as possible. This is an extremely serious matter that we are discussing, and Canadians have been wondering why parliament has not been more active before now in dealing with the strike.
The government has indicated that nothing concrete will happen at the conclusion of our debate. Tomorrow the strike will still be continuing and the millions of Canadians who need adequate postal services will continue to be denied them. What the debate will do is to allow us to put on record the fact that our constituents are demanding an

November 17, 1975
Postal Strike
end to this strike and that the time has come for the government to act.
My colleagues and I in the Progressive Conservative party for several weeks resisted pressures upon us to call for a legislated end to the strike because we believed that the collective bargaining process should be given every opportunity to work without parliament's intervention. It must be clear by now, however, that the strike will not end without parliament's intervention, and the time for us, to take action is now.
Every day that the strike continues brings more suffering for those least able to cope with its effects. For hundreds of thousands of retired Canadians this means that dividend cheques needed to pay for their rent or food are prevented from arriving, and that many of them with families abroad or long distances away have lost contact with their relatives.
For Canada's small businessmen the strike has cost millions of dollars already and the bill continues to mount each day the strike drags on. Before long many small businesses will be forced to close their doors because they simply cannot continue to carry unpaid bills for many more weeks. The cost will be high in terms of lost jobs and a declining rate of recovery from the present recession.
For the postal workers the strike has already cost each of them a considerable amount of money. One of the previous speakers used the figure of $1,000. For every Canadian, the added cost and inconvenience caused by this continuing strike will be great, and I believe that the protection of the public interest demands that the workers be sent back to work.
During the time I have been in Ottawa I have had a number of occasions when I spoke to protest the enormous inefficiency of the Post Office and the constantly increasing cost of this government department that is providing steadily declining levels of service. I have received hundreds of complaints from constituents about lost or delayed mail, or about the staggering waste of money spent to improve the public image of the Post Office. What is remarkable, however, is that virtually none of the complaints I have received has involved discourtesy or sloppiness on the part of the workers in our area. My experience is that our local workers have done more to enhance the reputation of the Post Office than any number of striped mail boxes or slick advertising campaigns.
What is disturbing is that morale among these workers has been declining along with the deterioration in the general level of service provided by the Post Office, because no amount of work on their part can make up for the breakdowns which occur in the postal system in our large cities. It is there that the greatest problem exists. My constituents feel the time has come for a complete re-evaluation of the Post Office and its activities. They are fed up with their mail being delayed for weeks on end. They are sick of receiving envelopes and parcels which have been torn open in transit and separated from their contents. And they feel there are better ways to spend the millions of dollars of taxpayers' money earmarked for advertising by the Post Office.

What the small businessmen in my area find particularly galling is that a government which is constantly picking their pockets, or showering them with miles of forms to fill out, or invading their businesses to scrutinize their books, or devising one new regulation after another, should prove so totally incapable of running its own operations. The simple fact is that if any businessman ran his operation the way the Post Office is being run, the government would have put him out of business long ago.
It should not be necessary to point out that the Post Office is an essential service in Canada. There is simply no other way of delivering the volume of parcels and messages that should be delivered by the Post Office if it were functioning. The reason for this is that the Post Office is the largest monopoly in the country and that, unlike the private monopolies and cartels which the government is quick to condemn, it is a coercive monopoly, one which enjoys the power of the law to protect its position. It is ironic in these circumstances that the former postmaster general has progressed from leading the country's largest monopoly to becoming Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet), a responsibility he discharges by travelling the countryside denouncing cartels and monopolies and threatening to jail businessmen.
The government cannot have it both ways. It cannot continue to maintain its monopoly position and then allow the essential services it is running to be shut down for long periods. Already this strike has been the longest in our postal history and no end to it is yet in sight. If the government is serious about ensuring that Canadians receive the service they deserve it will have to take a serious look at the alternatives available for the future. I say this because the average person will not stand for continued breakdown of the Post Office. Either the government will have to encourage private competition with the Post Office, or else it will be obliged to find new ways of settling labour-management disputes as well as dramatically upgrading the efficiency of the department.
Just this afternoon I was talking on the telephone with a small businessman in my constituency. He told me he wished he could find some method of getting his mail delivered that he could afford, because the delivery services presently operating are too expensive for small businesses to use. He was just one of thousands of cases where small businesses are being paralyzed by the postal strike.
I have spoken strongly in this House in support of civil rights which are being threatened. My stand on human rights is on record and I will continue to speak out in the future when I feel they are being infringed upon. But I have never believed that to deny the vast majority of people their right to essential services constitutes the human right of anyone, nor have I felt that a situation in which one party to an issue-in this case the government- could be Crown attorney, judge and jury, is one which can best lead to the solutions of our problems. When the welfare of our citizens can be held to ransom by a small group in an essential service there is no right to strike or lock out-there can only be the privilege to strike or lock workers out. It is time for that privilege to be withdrawn in the present situation, and for a fair and rational substitute to be put in place.
November 17, 1975

Over the last several months I have talked to a number of postal workers in my area. They are dedicated and hard-working; they did not want to strike. What they wanted was the opportunity to settle their differences with the government in a fair way without leaving their jobs. They were vexed by the fact that no negotiations for a new contract had taken place before their old contract ran out, and they were disturbed by the escalating war of words between the Postmaster General and the union leadership. They felt they deserved an increase in their salaries, those salaries having been eaten away by inflation and no longer being in line with those of people in similar jobs. I believe they were justified in seeking an increase.
They were also concerned about deteriorating working conditions in the Post Office and the sagging morale of the workers. Once again they were right in their worries, and they were correct too in deploring the use of television cameras in new facilities to monitor workers as though they were presumed to be thieves even before anything was missing.
What they were looking for was a way to solve their differences with management without having to engage in a strike which would gain them little and would serve only to enrage an increasingly hostile public. They knew that if they went on strike the government would be able to legislate them back to work on its own terms, but they could see little alternative to doing so. Already many of the people in my area have gone back to work. The Elmira post office, for example, re-opened on November 7, and the Orangeville workers have also returned to the job. I believe the workers would like to go back throughout most of Ontario and I think the union leadership is aware of this fact. Surely this is the reason they are doing whatever they can to prevent their membership having the opportunity to vote on the government's latest offer.
With the irresponsible and arrogant attitude of the present union leadership it is clear the postal workers will likely continue to be denied their right to vote. That is why I was disappointed that the leader of the NDP today prevented the House from accepting a motion which could have resulted in the rank and file of the union having the opportunity to decide what course of action would be followed now.
I listened to the hon. member's rationalisation on the radio this evening and I was disappointed that he should have sought to justify his opposition to the motion on the grounds that he saw it as a means of undermining the union leadership. He knows very well that such a vote could only bolster their position if they enjoyed anything like the support they claim to have. A vote on the contract could damage them only if they had been inflating the support they claimed from within the membership. I suspect that the leader of the NDP is aware of that fact, which is why he raised his voice in objection. In doing so he did a disservice both to the union membership and the Canadian public.
The government has the power to end this strike and it should do so before more time is lost. However, hon. gentlemen opposite must also demonstrate that they are aware of the more fundamental issues underlying the strike. They must recognize that negotiations for a new contract should begin long before the old contract expires. And they
Postal Strike
must recognize that the privilege of striking and locking out in essential services must, if the public interest is to be protected, be replaced by binding arbitration which would be fair to both workers and management and, most important of all, be fair to the Canadian public.
The government must show itself willing to deal with its workers on the basis of mutual trust. The closed circout television cameras now being used to spy on the workers should be removed from work areas. What is even more important, the government must show moral leadership both in the fight against inflation and in the restoration of a belief in the importance and dignity of work.
The government has created a social climate in which work thrift, and restraint are looked upon as a sucker's game. It has asked the working people to show restraint at the same time as it raids their earnings to pay for wasteful projects such as the senseless advertising campaign for the Post Office, costing more than $400,000, which included that meaningless advertisement showing a rural doctor mailing blood samples to the city. When I saw this advertisement I was shocked by this waste of money and I put a question on the order paper about it asking how much it had cost. The Postmaster General replied that it had cost $435,000. It included the suggestion that the Post Office feels "our mail is vital".
I asked the Postmaster General how many complaints of lost or damaged mail had been received by the Post Office in 1974 and his answer was that about 125,000 complaints had been received. I asked a further question-whether the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) was looking into the possibility of suing the Post Office for fraud, since it had claimed that the safe handling and delivery of Canadian mail was vital. The answer to that question was, no. It seems that fraud in government is quite different from fraud in the private sector; government would have acted more quickly there.
The Postmaster General should take a close look at the $2 million spent by the so-called public affairs group in the Post Office who are in fact nothing more than overpaid P.R. men for the Post Office.
If the government is to restore the work ethic in Canada it must also start to look at the unemployment insurance system which all too often subsidizes clever frauds at the expense of the working man, at the very same time as people who need help because they are sick or injured are refused it by the government. It should be remembered that, when we look at the malaise in the Post Office today, it was in the unemployment insurance program that the minister worked his last magic before turning his attention to the Post Office.
This strike must be ended now, and work must begin on overhauling the Post Office to turn it into a modern and efficient means of communication between Canadians and a rewarding place to work for the thousands of people it employs. Canadians are disturbed-as indeed they should be-by the fact that while the Post Office deficit has more than tripled in the past three years the quality of service has deteriorated badly. They have a right to demand leadership from the government, and if our efforts here tonight result in the re-appraisal of government policy toward the Post Office we will have achieved a great victory for the people of this country.

November 17, 1975
Postal Strike

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, much has been said here tonight. Words have poured undaunted from the mouths of many of my learned and very dignified colleagues.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext: But what do all these words mean? How many of the words spoken here tonight will be remembered when the lights are finally dimmed in these spacious surroundings? Will they all go for naught? Will these words, as so many times in the past, fall on deaf ears? I know they fall on deaf ears here. We look around from time to time and wonder who is listening.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext: We are listening.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext: I hope members on this side listen to what is said from the other side, and I hope that from time to time members over there stop hollering for long enough to listen to what is said on this side.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext: Get the whip to get your boys out.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext:
If there are so many of you who want to speak, there is no time limit on the debate and it can be allowed to go on until two o'clock tomorrow afternoon, in which case I am sure all will have their turn.
It is so easy for us here tonight to do what we are doing now, to wage political war on each other. What do we accomplish by this? Yet the words spoken in these political battles will be forgotten as surely as many of the words said here tonight will be forgotten within 24 hours.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext: You are turning it into a political arena.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext:
If you want to do that we can start right now. I do not have to repeat the message that has been repeated time and time and time again, both tonight and during the course of various stages of debate in the House of Commons. It is the voice of Canadians crying from one corner of the land to the other for reason. It is a voice crying for reason whether in this House, whether in the Post Office in the isolated outposts of the far north, in the far flung farms of the prairies, the fishing villages on both coasts, or the mighty metropolis up into the heart of Canada. What we are hearing throughout this debate is the cry to stop for a minute, listen, and look at the future.
There was a message on television tonight saying that the Canadian Labour Congress will start their $500,000 campaign to combat the government's anti-inflation measures tomorrow. I understand there will be buttons and ad compaigns, and the question we will be asked, which is one that the political leaders and the postal workers should take to heart, is: why me? That is the question that I think the letter carriers and every member of the postal workers' union is asking right now-why me? The answer is a very simple one.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext: They should ask that question in Toronto.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext: The hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) mentions Toronto.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext: I am telling you what the facts are.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext: It is nice to hear the facts from so learned and well educated a gentleman. I am sorry I do not have those qualifications. The answer to all of this has been fully revealed in our debate tonight. Each and every one of us is a Canadian concerned about the future of our country. If the postal workers ask why they should accept the package put forward at this time by the Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey), my answer to them and to the CLC, when they ask why me, is: because they are Canadians and their future depends on it. The future of this country depends on it.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext: Which side are you on?

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext:
You will never know. We are all concerned about the small businessman. Were the postal union members, in rejecting this contract, showing any concern for the rural mail carriers? I have not heard any member speak of them tonight, yet almost all of them depend upon the delivery of the mail to their areas. They are ready to go to work, and many of them are still at work. The previous speaker mentioned that a couple of postal stations are now open, and I commend them for that. Listowel has also been added to the list recently, and there are many others in western Ontario. Those of us who represent that part of the country can be proud of the fact that the people there take pride in their citizenship and in the fact that they want to work for a fair wage under reasonable conditions. But they do not ask the impossible.
Mail delivery in this country is something we could have been proud of over the years. Many members remember the importance of mail during the war years. Delivery of mail is important now particularly to small businesses in rural areas that not only do not have mail service but transportation to get mail delivered.
To the leaders of the postal workers I offer this old adage: By your actions you will be known. Let us look at some of the actions of the Canadian Union of Postal Workers. They want to be known as responsible citizens of this country. Is it responsible to hold 28 illegal stoppages of work in 30 months? What is responsible about that? What have they achieved by going out illegally 28 times in 30 months?
I think the one message we must take from the debate tonight is that there has been a response to the question: why me? Why should the union accept the contract? The answer is: because it is a good contract. It is a contract equal to one accepted by the letter carriers, one that in many respects is above the inflation guidelines.
Why cannot the government offer more? Simply because, as has been stated many times, we cannot afford to offer more. Many times people from my constituency-I am sure it is the same in other constituencies-have asked me when are we going to say no. Now is the time to say no, and there are many more times in the future when we will also have to say no. We must show determination and deliberateness by our actions tonight, and back up the Postmaster General in saying no. We must show him that
November 17, 1975

members of parties on both sides of the House are determined to back him up and continue to do so in the future. The answer for tonight, the answer for tomorrow, and the answer for the future, when someone asks "Why me?" is: because they are Canadians and it is their future we are talking about.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been listening with interest to the debate and I would like to add a few remarks.
The hon. member who spoke before me indicated, as other members before him and the Postmaster General himself, that the current offers are final. If the government decided they could do no more, we now ask for a decision to call those people back to work. For two or three years the situation had been deteriorating. Tonight's debate is concerned with postal workers. Not so long ago there was another postal strike. In other areas, proposals came quite short of meeting the Canadian people's needs and remedy both problems and inequities.
The minister explained he could not solve the problem because of exaggeration on the part of the union. But on the other hand, the postal service has been paralyzed for five or six weeks. We recognize this is an essential service. How long are we going to ponder the issue of essential services and the public interest? Such in my view is the question every member should ask himself. I realize the minister made every effort to reach a settlement.
We recognize the public is faced with serious difficulties because of the postal stoppage. This afternoon again we received representations, as so many others did. In my village, the manager of a very important business firm in the area indicated he was establishing a collection service for the twelve hundred accounts to be collected during the month. There are a large number of such firms across the country.
Last week I was concerned that the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer) announced the introduction of an emergency service to move correspondence and also family allowance and old age security cheques, and I wondered whether the government was preparing to maintain the status quo for a long time, and that service will apparently cost at least $700,000 a month. Up to what point will that service enable the government to maintain the status quo?
However, we believe that considering all the efforts the minister made and the objections of the union, the government should take responsible action. We were asked in the evening what the opposition wanted. We want the government to take responsible action, to meet the needs of the public, and we sincerely believe that dispute could drag on for quite a long while. Some hon. members suggested mediation, we suggested a free vote of all the workers interested considering the present government offers. If all that fails, we shall then be willing to consider special legislation to bring workers back to work with a mind to public interest.
Postal Strike
Mr. Speaker, I will with your permission quote some editorials and especially the one by Claude Ryan who recently declared:
However, that is not the fundamental question the Canadian people put to the Postmaster General today ... The only question that should interest them is in fact this one: How long can the country be sensibly left to live without a postal service in the name of public interest?
That is the question we are trying to deal with tonight.
As long as a strike is liable to produce better results than bargaining, and as the public weal can put up with it more or less, a government may be justified in allowing a work stoppage affecting a great public service to go on. But neither condition is present in this dispute.
First, according to the government itself, there is no chance postal workers will get higher salary offers than those about which they have already been told. For over a month, the government has stood firmly by the recommendations of the Moisan report. Since they already go beyond the guidelines of the anti-inflation program, any further increase would be an unthinkable blow at this time to the credibility of the government.
Second, there is also the incalculable damage that the strike causes to thousands of individuals and businesses. Many undertakings, either by the very nature of their business or because of their abundant financial resources, can quickly learn to do without the Post Office. However, this is not true for hundreds of others for whom the Post Office is an absolutely essential service. A newspaper like Le Devoir used to have nearly 20,000 mail subscribers; the famous reform launched under Mr. Kierans was to make it lose several thousands. But those it still has face for the second time in less than a year a deprivation of service directly attributable to the paralysis of the Post Office. Now what about the incomes of hundreds of businesses? In a large number of businesses called upon to transact with hundreds and thousands of individual clients, the near totality of accounts receivable are usually collected through the mail. For a newspaper, this is true particularly for subscription renewals. Is Mr. Mackasey unaware that for the past three weeks cash receipts have been reduced to their simplest expression while salaries and suppliers still have to be paid?
If postal workers cannot expect anything more from an indefinite prolongation of their work stoppage and the damage done to the public good by their strike continues to increase, there remains only one solution to the dispute: the government must reaffirm without delay the priority of the general good over the exercise by a particular group of a right whose effectiveness in this case has now been reduced to nothing.
Mr. Vincent Prince stated in turn:
It must not be forgotten that certain normative clauses have considerable financial implications and that this expedient should not be used to win gains that would go against Ottawa's new salary policy.
Indeed, this bargaining is the first significant test of the austerity measures. We can take it for granted that the federal government will be specially watchful.
Moreover, an extended strike would not affect the public and postal workers alone. The mailmen and drivers of postal vans laid off, because they were temporarily useless, will apparently have to be satisfied with unemployment insurance. They will become part of the majority taken as hostage.
I would like to quote some comments that I find much to the point. In today's La Presse, Mr. Guay states:
The Trudeau government has set a ceiling on price and income increases. If it is consistent with itself, it need not tergiversate about granting wage increases to postal workers as to all other government employees. In the interest of business, taxpayers and the majority of postal workers, the government has the responsibility to order the strikers back to work. In fact, it is unworthy of a government to allow a strike to last this long to break a union. Moreover, it is an absurd mistake that reflects a superficial analysis of social realities. Unions are not broken today as they were fifty years ago. On the other hand, government must set the example to play fair and to display dignity. It must not lower itself to the level of some union leaders' demagogic maneuvers. Even though the postal workers' union leaders are apt to

November 17, 1975
Postal Strike
use the government's order to return to work to save and even consolidate their prestige with their members, the government must not be distracted by such mean considerations.
Those are comments I consider appropriate, Mr. Speaker. I find them relevant, because we have reason to wonder if it is not that fight that drags on between the recognized union and the government. Which one could lose face? I wonder how far should be put away the responsibility or the theory of the face loser, considering the importance of the conflict.
I must congratulate the mover to have proposed the debate to the House, considering the problems involved. We ask the government to bring back order to the postal service. We are not accusing the minister of not having tried, but we think that the time has come for those workers to go back to work. For a very long time, we have been asking ourselves very serious questions in the public sector. We must surely think about the matter of essential services. As for essential services, Mr. Speaker, I have very personal opinions on that subject.
In the eventuality of a refusal on the part of the unions, I feel a special act should be passed to stabilize and restore an economy which is now seriously ill in Canada. How long will the government hesitate to meet that need, and answer the representations we have made this evening?
The government assumed the responsibility of giving a leadership that will encourage Canadians. We spoke of the pessimism of Canadians a while ago. We said that Canadians were concerned about the future of this country, that it was completely normal to worry about the future of our country, if we look at what has been going on for the last four or five years and consider the hesitations of the government to commit itself with regard to various measures. We are up against the problem of inflation and we are still waiting for steps to remedy the situation.
Moreover, we are hit by those strikes that harm our economy and take place in the public sector. Parliament gave the unions the right to strike. The government side always accuses us of being against the right to strike, but every time there has been a strike in the public sector, that paralyzed our economy, which harmed and hampered our society, a special act has always been introduced. If that is not denying the union members the right to strike, I wonder what is.
Let us be honest, let us not be hypocrites. I feel the time has come to reflect seriously on the right to strike. Will we have to reconsider privilege granted the union members, to the extent where they abuse it? I am asking this question both to my colleagues and hon. members opposite: Have we seriously considered what services are really essential? Mr. Speaker, we would need to establish new ways and demonstrate creativity to offer union members a fair treatment. Someone has mentioned a labour court. I am thinking about offices with a permanent bargaining court. I feel that we should think of necessity about the establishment of new procedures, because those we have now lead us too often into dilemmas such as the one we are in today.
If, on the one hand, unions show a lack of good will and refuse to co-operate in the interest of Canada, every government, including this Parliament, not only has the right but the duty to react by offering an alternate solution, so that we are now asking ourselves serious questions. I, for

one, am asking it, together with many in my constituency with whom I have talked about this issue. People often ask: What is the government doing? What is the government doing to do? We are sick of these problems.
Is it necessary to remind the government of their responsibilities? Is it necessary to remind the government that we will support any measure which could reduce the difficulties faced by Canadians now? Is it necessary to be sure that the government did more than their best to find solutions? But given the ill will of some individuals, of some spokesmen for groups who definitely do not represent the interest of the community, I think the time has come to take decisions, and this evening or more precisely, this morning, we ask the government to react quickly to this matter which annoys so many Canadians. And we think that the government should react immediately by proposing mediation or by passing special legislation if the mediator's report were unacceptable to the union members, while hoping that the government would accept the report of a mediator who, in the short term, could find the solution. This would enable both parties to end the conflict and save faces. Mr. Speaker, I shall be brief because other colleagues have some remarks to make, but I hope that the problem will be settled and that we will think more in terms of the future. Taking into account the experiences we have been through, we must consider seriously these new mechanisms, and I feel it is up to the government to study carefully this matter and find solutions. And inasmuch as those solutions will respect individuals and meet the needs of a society we would like to see better, I am sure the government will listen attentively. That is, Mr. Speaker, what we want most.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, never before have I heard so many members speak on a subject about which they do not know anything. Regretfully I say I join that class.
While you and I, Mr. Speaker, have had some experience with labour, I think we would be very presumptuous if we decided we could look at a situation affecting a union with which we have never been directly involved, and about which we know very little, and say we have a solution which would be satisfactory to anyone.
I am surprised at the attitude of the Progressive Conservative party which seems to be: let us pass legislation and put them back to work and that will solve the problem. That would not solve the problem. Part of the problem is that the workers have never had sufficient guts to go on strike or in any way involve themselves in a collective agreement until the past few years. These people, in many segments of our economy, are not accustomed to negotiating contracts and co-operating with each other. They have never been very much involved with the idea of unionism which, to some extent, is represented by the phrase you are your brother's keeper and only through solidarity can you help to achieve what you wish.
Frankly I have been surprised by the attitude of so many members who believe they can legislate a settlement to this problem which would produce a reasonable mail service in this country. I do not think this can happen. I have listened to many of the remarks that have been made.
November 17, 1975

I was very impressed by the young hopeful of the Ontario Liberal party, the federal member who claims he intends to seek the leadership. I owe him a vote of thanks because I never really looked at my own colleagues in terms of their being different, but they certainly are. The number of degrees that my colleagues have, surprised me. I suppose that from now on I will have to pay them more respect because of their great educational achievements. But I was surprised that he did not know several things.
For instance, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) was a member of a union for 50 years or so, and he had been active in that union. He participated in it, and is still paying his dues today. I would think that when he pays those dues he must give some consideration to that union. Another one of my colleagues has been active in union work for a number of years and has been connected with a number of unions in the clothing industry. I think he probably has a little experience in it by now. But because we have had some experience does not mean we really know how to solve this very vexing problem.
I have great respect for the Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey) but it has surprised me that he has taken it on himself to solve a problem that has been developing in the Post Office over the last 30 or 40 years, and is trying to solve that problem all at once. I am not only referring to money-I will mention that in a few moments. The Postmaster General has tried to solve these problems in a very forceful way, and he has acted as a true employer in some ways when he said that that is as far as he will go. He has issued that ultimatum on television a number of times. He has forced the workers to look at the situation, and I think this was a good idea.
He has been sympathetic with regard to some of the aspects of the situation which have been mentioned but that are worth mentioning again. One of them is the changes in the Post Office. One of the young members today mentioned the skills of the postal people. In the past they used card boxes and filing cases. They knew the routes and the streets. It is a highly skilled occupation and they are proud of their skill. Then we introduced automation. We paid absolutely no attention to the downgrading of the person who had been doing that highly skilled job, and we substituted a machine for him.
I do not know whether the postal code works. I boycott it because I do not believe it works. I do not believe that a machine can sort out a code written by pen, or pencil, or ballpoint, in whatever style of writing you have. It would have to be written in a specific place on that envelope with a certain kind of ink, because that is how cheques work in a bank. I know that the postal code could be typed and that that could work.
The worker in the Post Office has been very concerned about whether or not he will have a job and, much more important, whether than job will be important and will give him a sense of accomplishment. In my opinion the Postmaster General has given this problem some attention. He has also given attention to the problem of surveillance.
It seems to me it is going a little far to have workers going to the washroom surveilled, unless you are making
Postal Strike
blue movies. I think that with the use of other methods and with greater trust we can develop a better class of person who will no longer need to be spied upon and treated in a less than humane way, and then the job will be done that much better.
There have been an immense number of grievances in the Post Office which have never been dealt with, or at least only at negotiation time. This is happening all across the nation. Everyone is upset because teachers are going on strike, postal workers are going on strike, and garbage collectors are going on strike. All these people have been treated as less than human beings. They were part of the machine. You, Mr. Speaker, and I who have been in major craft unions were treated as individuals and we were proud of the jobs we did.
I was an underground hard-rock miner for many years. It was the top job in the mine, one of the most dangerous and best paid jobs. It was a job I was proud of doing. When I went home at night I knew I had done a good day's work. For that one had the respect of one's employer and one's fellow employees, and everyone in that industry did a good job or they did not stay very long. I sat on negotiation committees for years. The members of those committees were as interested in the guy who was the powder-monkey or the old chap who was working on a pipe fitting gang. They were as interested in the lowest paid person in the plant as they were in the best paid or the highest skilled, simply because we knew that solidarity was the name of the game and we had to stick together.
We are doing something else right now with regard to the Post Office. I would like to ask the Postmaster General whether he could guarantee on behalf of the government, if the union agrees to a supervised vote on the Treasury Board's final offer, that if it is rejected no government action will be taken but that negotiations would be reopened through mediation or in any other way, and a settlement reached. If that happened it is quite likely that the postal workers would get no benefits from it because it would have to go before the Anti-inflation Board which may well reject it because it might go beyond the guidelines and beyond the historical relationship with the other agencies, but it would be fair and in that way the workers would get as much as they can get.
I am surprised at the free enterprisers in the House who always talk about free enterprise. That is what the labour movement is in the north American context. It is a free enterprise operation. The company makes as much money as it can make, and the union demands as much money for its workers as it can. They are not taking a moral position and it has nothing to do with the co-operative idea. You get from the employer as much as you can on behalf of the people for whom you are bargaining.
I suggest that what we are doing now is to put this union-and this will apply to other unions in the future- under double jeopardy because we say they should vote on the government offer, but if they take that vote and if it turns out that the union accepts the vote, everybody will be happy, except perhaps for the leaders of the union who may not have recommended it. If they reject it, what do we do then? We pass legislation and put them back to work.

November 17, 1975
Postal Strike
I suggest if we ask them to do this-if the government asks them to conduct a vote on its last offer, then the government should be prepared to say that if the offer is rejected it will continue the negotiations to arrive at a settlement, and then the Anti-Inflation Board can look at it. It could reject it or accept it, but we would have concluded negotiations in the normal way.
It seems to me that the statements that have been made about how this strike is hurting small businesses and individuals are very important. It is a fact that businesses are in very serious difficulty because of this strike. I am sure this is true of any strike, certainly of those in the public sector. I think I agree with a statement the Postmaster General has made on a number of occasions, however, to the effect that when this strike is over the relationship on both sides should be good enough so that we can really start to negotiate with the Post Office employees. It should also be good enough that the postal service will return to the standard it gave previously.
We hear of sabotage, of theft, and all sorts of things in the Post Office today. It would appear to me that if we took the motion that was proposed earlier and legislated these people back to work there would be a deterioration in our national mail service. In my opinion, we cannot afford to have it deteriorate any more. The settlement will have to be acceptable to the average Joe working in that operation otherwise it does not matter whether it satisfies the government, satisfies the union leadership, members of parliament, or some little old lady in the Pas who cannot get her medicine. I do not think this really matters.
If we are going to achieve reason on both sides, from that will come the machinery with which to make the changes that have to be made in the Post Office. For instance, junk mail should not be given to carriers on Monday morning when they have the Friday, Saturday and Sunday mail. Only the first class mail should be taken out on Monday morning instead of everything, as one postmaster insisted on doing recently.
It seems to me that we can provide a decent service in Canada but we have not been getting it. I strongly recommend to members that forcing the strikers back to work will not accomplish our objective of a better mail service. We should have that even if we have to pay for it. Equating our money with that of other countries, a 12 cent first class postage charge would not be unreasonable-providing we could supply the standard of first class mail service we had 20 years ago.

Do

Mr. Speaker, I cannot speak for the government but I can speak for myself. First of all, we would have to supervise the vote. Perhaps this supervising could be done even by members of the press gallery or somebody neutral who would see that the vote was properly held. We would have to make sure that there was proper explanation of the settlement to the workers, namely, that if they put in the hours they have over the past three years they would earn anywhere from $14,000 to $17,000. If the vote went the way of the leadership, obviously the leaders would come back to the bargaining table in a much stronger position.
I would not want to mislead the House and say there does not come a moment when you have to put public interest above private interest, or that we would never legislate them back, but I can guarantee we would get back to the bargaining table.
I have no knowledge of which way the Anti-Inflation Board would go if, through that additional strength, the unions were able to bargain more money. I was impressed with the hon. gentleman's speech but I should like to ask him a question: you cannot compensate with money for bad conditions, or does he think you can?

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext: I am in total agreement with that, Mr. Speaker. There is always a conflict when negotiating the conditions of work-hours and holidays and other things. You relate fringe benefits to the package that money is in. I agree entirely with the Postmaster General that money will not compensate for the other things. I think the rancour that may be created by back-to-work legislation would do the same thing-that rancour would be very difficult to overcome. Even if money were available subsequently, the damage would be such that the postal service would not be adequate or what we anticipate.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at this time of morning hon. members may wonder if a debate like this serves any useful purpose. Having listened to a good deal of it, I think it has been a useful debate with useful contributions from all sides. I cannot say that I agree in total, or even in large measure, with some of the things said this evening, but I think in totality the House has gained a good deal of insight with respect to this difficult situation. I think we have also given the Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey) a number of specific points to consider as well as those involved on the union side.
It was mentioned earlier that some of the senior negotiators were here this evening. I know they will read with interest the totality of the debate. I am not going to add too much new information but I want to focus on three or four areas of great importance and of some controversy.
November 17, 1975

One point in particular seems to be the importance of the strike itself, or the importance of the loss of postal service. Partly because of the fact that this is not a new experience, that there have been, I think, 16 postal strikes since 1967, it has been possible for the Postmaster General and others to say that people have become used to the situation. I think what has really happened is that people have been in a constant state of traumatization. They never knew from week to week, or month to month, whether they were going to have a postal service that would function.
The minister said that the direct mail business people are in favour of a long strike to clear the air. I presume that if many have expressed a similar opinion there is support for that point of view. But let me utter a word of caution. I am not sure that the confrontation approach, this talk of clearing the decks or, to use the phrase of the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. MacFarlane), of being on the beach, is valid or convincing. I think the hon. member was using a war analogy. I am too young to be fully cognizant of its meaning. At any rate, such military-type solutions will do little.
Some talk of "if and when" the strike is settled. I think there is more at stake than simply allowing people to go to the wall. Some think that once we have driven people to the wall, once we have gone through the valley of the shadow, as it were, somehow everything will be set right. I am sure that is not the minister's position. He has had much experience ironing out labour-management problems, and I am sure that is not what he means.
I am disturbed by statements made inside and outside the House that, somehow or other, the strike is not serious. We have embarked on some crazy debates about small businessmen and others, but never said a strike is not serious. This is the second largest country in the world, although thinly populated with some 22 million people. We are all linked, on economic, social and cultural terms, with a basic mail service. Suspending mail service for four weeks does basic damage to the fabric of our country.
Perhaps all our people are not overly concerned. Perhaps those living in an urban community, to whom most amenities are available within a few square miles, can get along without postal service. They have available newspapers, radio, television, courier service, and can travel from place to place in their limited geographic locality. But this does not hold true for a large percentage of our people. I represent a part of the country which depends greatly on mail service. We depend on the Post Office day by day, week by week, and do not want to be without the service one hour, one minute longer than absolutely necessary.
Frankly I deeply resent arguments made inside and outside this House that this going to the wall, this knock-them-down-once-and-for-all strike, will resolve all the difficulties the Post Office has experienced in recent years. I do not think that is true. It is a simplistic position at best. At worst it is exceedingly dangerous, as such a position involves the denial of a basic service provided to the citizens of this country. In all honesty I must ask why the Postmaster General in this instance has adopted a position highly unusual for the government.
Postal Strike
As hon. members know, I have been here ten years. During those years when there were work stoppages in this country's public service the government ended the work stoppages through legislation. This was done with grain handlers, seaway workers, and railway employees. The minister suggested we have never done this with our own employees. We have always done it, so to speak, as disinterested third parties when employees of Crown corporations or other entities have been involved. Technically, he is quite right, but the technical argument carries little weight with me because I am not a lawyer. My training is that of a theologian, which may not always be useful in solving some of the problems we encounter in this House.
Why is the minister advancing basically a lawyer's argument? Usually he does not adopt such rationale. Why is he doing it with respect to the Post Office, considering his great experience as Minister of Labour in the settling of difficult labour-management negotiations? Why, in a sense, is the government adopting a new position on this particular strike?
True, a number of times he said, "We will not legislate our own employees back to work." But I do not find his argument convincing. Surely his decision is based on something more substantial than a legal nicety. There are two possibilities, one of which was referred to long before this evening. I do not want to sound unpleasant, but it seems to me that the minister wants to discredit the leadership of CUPW.

speechtext: They do not need my help.

speechtext:
My colleague has put it even more strongly. My suggestion might be part and parcel of the minister's position; I hope he will explain if that is so. Others conclude, and perhaps this is closer to the mark, that the minister wants to work within the government's anti-inflation program. After all, he had considerable experience as Minister of Labour in bringing about settlements; perhaps he thinks the time has come to alter a basic aspect of labour-management relations in the public service, the legislated settlement.
Apparently the minister wants to change the sort of thing that happened in the past. In the public service we have witnessed negotiations, the breakdown of negotiations, the appointment of an outside mediator who filed a report, further discussions and, finally, a strike. The strike continues sometimes for five or ten days, or two weeks, after which there is a legislated settlement. Employees in the public service have become increasingly aware of the possibilities of a final, legislated settlement. They know that if they go on strike for a few days they will not be without pay long enough to be badly hurt and that parliament will finally legislate them back to work. If the minister is trying to cure that mentality through this particular strike, I say he is playing a dangerous game. He is, in a sense, trying to deal with questions concerning labour-management relations in the Post Office without going to the root causes, to which reference was made earlier this evening.
I think the minister is too much imbued with his previous role as Minister of Labour, when he was successful in achieving strike settlements. He operated as a kind of lone gun who could wait them out if necessary, going into all

November 17, 1975
Postal Strike
night bargaining sessions in shirt sleeves, ready to strike when the iron was hot, ready to pull a settlement out of the fire. It was very much a kind of "by the seat of your pants" operation. He received favourable credit for being a success at it.
The minister has reached the point now where he may be well over his head. He may well be playing fast and loose with a vital service service such as the Post Office which will find it very difficult to recover from this kind of "High Noon" treatment. I do not say this with any kind of enthusiasm, but quite frankly the minister has reached the stage where he better accept some serious counsel from other people who understand the two or three issues he is trying to deal with at the same time and in the same capsule.
It strikes me that the game the minister is playing is such a dangerous one, and one that is so uncertain of being successful, it has to be one he should not pursue at any greater length unless he believes there is absolutely no other route to follow. I do not believe that is true.
There have been a number of suggestions. They have been made by my colleague, the hon. member for Vancouv-er-Quadra (Mr. Clarke), who put before the minister this evening a number of possibilities that are well worthy of consideration. The Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) made a suggestion which deserves more than summary disapproval of the minister. A few moments ago the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) made a further suggestion to which the minister should give some consideration.
The time has come for the minister to realize that to use this device of this strike, either to reorganize the authority structure of CUPW, or to establish new precedents with regard to legislative intervention by this parliament, is not the name of the game with respect to the restoration of postal service. The time has long since passed for the minister to confer with the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and his colleagues and to say that there are two or three options which will achieve a conclusion to this very difficult and very costly strike, and they must be acted upon here and now.
If there is anything useful to the special debate we have had this evening it is that the minister will realize at the conclusion of the debate, which will come in the next hour or two, that the time for sitting and hoping for other than these things to happen is not going to occur. The time for him and his colleagues to exercise their responsibility has arrived. A number of options have been placed before the minister this evening. It is his duty and the duty of the government to act upon them, and to act upon them now.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I look at the clock I feel we have good cause to ask ourselves what we are doing here at this hour. Our very presence here at this time, dealing with this subject, is the strongest and most convincing argument I can imagine of the importance of our present debate.
The Post Office is in real trouble. The Canadian public expects us to do something about it. That is why we are here. We should express our thanks, all of us, to the hon.

member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke) for precipitating this discussion.
In order to understand the full significance of our presence here and our discussion of this matter, we must go back to a few real basics in the matter of collective bargaining. For example, I read in an article in the May 3 edition of the Montreal Star that the failures in collective bargaining created a need for a new approach. That is a sort of beginning.
The basics that we really must be looking at start with the concept that the Public Service is hired by the public to provide a service to the public. It is almost a tautology to say so, but it is essential we understand that is what it is all about. When that service is withdrawn or offered in offhand manner, the public feels cheated. The public pays for the service. When it is deprived of it, it is quite understandably annoyed, frustrated, and wants something done about it.
The reasons for withdrawing the service have to be determined. It may be the intransigence on the part of the union or intransigence on the part of the spokesman for the public.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext: Or both.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext:
It may be a mixture of both. Let us remember that there is a proxy in both cases. There is a surrogate spokesman; a surrogate for the people offering the service and a surrogate for the people demanding the service. These people think they are interpreting their constituents. They should not necessarily think that they are always correct in this.
When the public interest is seriously affected he who is in the wrong has to be brought to task, the union or the government, the negotiators on one side or the other, in order to restore service to the public, which in the final analysis is the employer in this particular situation. The determination may not be easy, but it is one that has to be made.
Much has been said in this debate this evening about strikes and the right to strike. I would like to say a word or two about another aspect of strikes that must, in my opinion, be brought to a halt. It is not inherent in any right to strike. To my way of thinking it is an aberration. I refer, of course, to picketing. Picketing is a denial of man's right to make individual decisions and carry them out. Picketing can be used to draw attention to an alleged grievance. That is a legitimate form of picketing. However, when picketing is carried to the length of causing harm to people who legitimately want to return to work, it becomes, morally anyway, unlawful. It should be made unlawful. We are the people who can do so.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext: No way.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext:
I hear "no way". Just you wait. In this morning's paper I read that a woman in Montreal legitimately wanted to go back to work. She was hurt as she tried to go through the picket line to go back to her legitimate job. She has every right to do that. She wants to earn her wage. Why shouldn't she? Why should a picket stop her from doing so?

We have been talking about abridging the right to strike, putting brackets around it or limiting it in some way. We must also consider that there is no right to picket and keep people from doing the job they have been hired to do.
As to the strike itself, the strike, we all remember, is one of those elements in the collective bargaining system which was granted by an earlier Liberal government-I notice there is no applause-against the advice of the chairman of the Civil Service Commission of that day. The Heeney Report advised strongly against according the right to strike to the public service. The government of the day in its "wisdom"-and I put that word in quotation marks-decided there should be a right to strike written into the Public Service Staff Relations Act, and there it is. I have never understood just why it should be so.
I was a member of the public service at that time. I never asked for it. I would be ashamed to exercise it. I do not think it needs to be there. However, as a means of upholding the public interest in these circumstances and recognizing in the final analysis that the public is the employer, I have tried since I have been in parliament a variety of routes in the Joint Committee on Employer-Employee Relations in the Public Service to see what now needs to be done to reduce the damage which was done by extending the right to strike to the public service. That right is there, but it needs to be fenced in; it needs to be limited because obviously it has not worked properly.
I tried a variety of forms, a variety of propositions. One of them was to suggest in the committee that we withdraw the right to strike from the public service. I was told I was dreaming in technicolour-the expression was used earlier today but it was another member of the Committee who used it on that occasion. Obviously I would not be able to obtain majority support for that notion, so I tried another approach. It involved an elaboration of the Public Interest Disputes Commission which ended up in arbitration. This did not attract much approval so I tried a third approach.
My third approach had to do with liability, the notion being that, once it is determined who is responsible for the service being suspended, that entity should become liable for the damage done to the individual, to the person who wants to service; that the government on the one hand, if it is responsible, or the employee, the employee's union on the other, should be held liable to be sued for the damage which has been done to the public-to individual members of the public.
We have all heard this evening about the various kinds of damage to the public caused by a strike of the present nature. This idea, I was told, was so complicated that it would tie up the courts endlessly from now until the end of the 21st century. Again I was informed this was a no-starter.
Then there was a suggestion from one of our members who was not able to be there. A discussion was prompted and it brought forward the notion which was mentioned this evening by one hon. member, which came to the point of suggesting that we should have inserted in the law-and I am breaking no confidence now, he broached the matter earlier-provision for a secret ballot not only on the strike but on the decision to hold a strike vote. I think this ought
Postal Strike
to be done also, because there is always too much danger to an individual member of a union should he stand up and say, "I oppose a strike." He may oppose a strike, but when he gets home he finds his windows broken. Unfortunately this happens. I am not suggesting it is happening to a marked extent in this situation, but it does happen. The individual must be protected.
Too little has been said this evening about the damage which has been done to the public which has been paying for the service. The damage has been grievous. It would have been serious at any time of the year. It is even more serious at Christmastime when, for example, the United Appeal campaigns are in full spate. Christmas seals are being sold and other community welfare campaigns are operating. Many of our local community services are likely to be severely handicapped in 1976 as a result of this strike.
Many of the small businesses across the country are running into difficulties. One case immediately comes to mind, because when I was home over the weekend I happened to drop into a variety store where a man had bought his stock of Christmas cards. He has $3,000 worth of Christmas cards on his hands and nobody is buying them. He is only one of thousands who had ordered supplies in plenty of time-they were delivered by transport of one kind or another. So he has either to service the debt to pay for his purchase or he must take it out of his capital stock. This is a serious matter for the man affected by it, but it is only symptomatic of the damage being done to businesses.
It is true arrangements are being made to distribute social security cheques. But travellers, and those who are looking for their passports are greatly inconvenienced. How many of us are carrying passports back and forth? I hope we all are. I am. The purchasers of Canada Savings Bonds are having their problems. Some people who bought Canada Savings Bonds did so as a form of immediate saving intending to cash them as soon as they were delivered. But they are not being delivered. I know a person who wanted to put down a number of bonds as a down payment on the purchase of a house on November 1. He could not get them. I am still looking for them. He probably missed a chance to get that house, or else he was obliged to pay a much higher mortgage rate.
We cannot avoid the conclusion that the public interest is deeply affected and that it is the duty of the government to restore the service and see that it is maintained. This could be done by back-to-work legislation for which we have called. I would point out that we have not pushed this point of view too hard, realizing that delicate negotiations were in progress; we did not want those negotiations to be destroyed or thrown out of balance. Nevertheless the time has come, not only for back-to-work legislation but for legislation accompanied by a requirement for a vote of confidence in the executive of the union and for the negotiating team which worked out the settlement. In this way we could restore the postal service to what it should be and then, when the time comes, when the report from the Joint Committee on Employer-Employee Relations comes down, we hope we shall be given legislation which will restore proper working relations between the government, as proxy for the public, and the unions so that relations between those two important aspects of our society may be restored.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in determining whether I should speak in this debate and trying to assess whether or not anything any of us could say would make any impact on the government, what determined me to make a brief speech even at this later hour was a phrase the Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey) used when he began his speech. He said that people can adjust psychologically to this strike.
I think the key to the thinking of the Postmaster General is contained in the word psychologically. Surely asking the Canadian people to make such an adjustment in a service which, as we have heard so many times tonight, is an essential service, one that the Canadian people not only have a right to but have a great and in many cases desperate need for, is to give the Canadian people the kind of government that they do not deserve. The Canadian people deserve a parliament that is not spending its time legislating grain handlers, air traffic controllers, longshoremen, airport firefighters, and now, because of hopeless deadlock, the postal workers, back to work.
The Postmaster General has said that people are not complaining, that they can make adjustments. He ought to come to my office in Edmonton and hear the personal complaints of businessmen and people who need the mails. If he did, he would not have such a lacklustre attitude.
I am not going to dwell on this point; it has been made many times tonight. I merely say that if there is insecurity, uncertainty, alienation, and frustration in Canadian society today, it is because of the absence of strong leadership by a government that will take the economic situation in its grip and do something to help businesses and people maintain economic stability.
How much longer do we need to have a strike before convincing the government that without strong action on its part the postal service will not be resumed? For reasons somewhat surreptitious, as the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald) said in his intervention this evening, the government has decided not to bring into the House at this point back-to-work legislation. It will not even bring in legislation calling for a mandatory vote by the membership of the union on the government's latest offer.
We have said enough tonight to satisfy ourselves that without the continued protests of members of parliament, who are doing their best to convince the government it is on the wrong course, we would be remiss in our duty. This is why so many of us have stood up tonight. The government seems to be concerned with protecting the democracy of a few union leaders at the expense of the democracy of the Canadian people.
We have as much right to the continuation of essential services as the union leadership has the right to try to hold a gun at our heads. There will come a time when the Canadian people will finally rear up and resist the continued breakdown of society as a result of strikes. I believe that in the interdependent society that Canada has become from east to west and all through the various reaches and avenues of our life, the strike has become an outmoded weapon. The best union leaders of North America themselves are saying that the strike is outmoded.

Why then do we persist with paying tribute to the alleged sacredness of the strike? I suggest it is time we go far beyond that. I think it is why we in parliament ought to be thinking beyond the mere settlement of this strike. I have heard this kind of speech before from members of parliament. They say "Let us get by this strike situation we are in, and bring in better legislation so we will not get ourselves into this box again." But when are we going to learn? Having said that strikes are outmoded in essential services, I go on to suggest that strikes be prohibited. The Canadian people want an end to strikes in essential services.
Just what is an essential service can be defined by a public commission. Let some of the best people in the country be appointed to a commission to determine what is an essential service. Believe you me, Mr. Speaker, the money we pay them would be more than repaid by what will be saved by preventing continued economic disruptions because of strikes in essential services. With such an arrangement surely our bargaining process would reach the point where, if there were failure to agree on the terms of a contract in a declared essential service, the dispute could be sent to a labour court, a public commission, or an impartial arbitration body empowered to make a fair judgment.
I believe such a system is worth a try. It certainly is not new. Many people have talked about it for years but no one in this country will do it. The Canadian people deserve far better treatment than they are now getting. They deserve a sense of urgency on the part of government. They do not deserve to be told by the Postmaster General that they can simply adjust psychologically and start using telex and the telephone, and life can go on. Life cannot go on in the way Canadian people want it to go on, and it is time the Postmaster General was told that plainly.
