I think the Postmaster General is perfectly right in not wanting to get into the same kind of box some of his colleagues are in by paying one group of workers more than another group. You cannot do that without getting into a mess, and I happen to agree with the Postmaster General in that regard.
The Postmaster General should realize that one of the reasons why the employees are prepared to go on strike has nothing to do with dollars and cents. Even with a settlement on the basis of the offer by the Postmaster General, there are still thousands of employees in the Post Office Department who are being put upon, who are fed up, who do not have any protection, and over whom the union has no jurisdiction at all.
The Postmaster General sits back and accepts memos from the Post Office brass, but he does not go out and talk to some of the people who have been casuals for eight, nine and 12 years. These people are not casuals, they are casualties of the Postmaster General. I thought he was to be the one to correct these things. We have waited all these months for him to do something. I am sure the Postmaster General would be very happy if a vote could be taken that did not support the union, and the leadership was dissipated overnight. I am sure he would be very happy about that.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit one question? Does the hon. gentleman know that one of the requests of the union at the bargaining table is to eliminate all casuals?

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext: Yet he is telling me at the same time that they are fighting for more casuals.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext:
No, that is not what I am telling you. The Postmaster General was not listening. I am telling the

Postmaster General there is dissatisfaction in the union ranks in the Post Office Department, and whether the grievance involves casuals or part time employees, if he would check the records of management and of the union right across the country he would find that there are thousands of cases still unsettled. That is what I am telling him. Whatever agreement he reached with the union in respect of casuals, they do not trust him or believe him. I would seem to me he might do a few things about some of the old cases that are on the books.
If the minister wants to earn the trust not only of the rank and file members of the department but of the union leadership he will kick the ass out of some of his management types, and get the old things settled and out of the way. When is he going to do this? I get sick and tired of him telling us he has been a union member, and so on. It seems to me he has forgotten where he came from and that he has forgotten why he is here. Some of the men and women in the Regina post office tell me they look upon him as the typical free enterprise bureaucrat with a great big "B". They have some picayune grievances. They are not big things, but they are angry about them. Where has he been? He serves ultimatums. He is the big wheel who has forgotten about the bargaining process.
Until the Postmaster General returns to where he came from he will continue to have grievances in the Post Office Department, just as his predecessors had. I have not seen much improvement since he took over the portfolio from his predecessors. I submit to the Postmaster General that if he would get a lot of these things which add up to much anger and frustration among his and other employees out of the way, he would receive co-operation from the employees of the Post Office Department.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to speak tonight but I shall do so for two or three minutes because of the speech of the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin).
The hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Roche) asked earlier, "Will they learn"? I wonder when the members of the NDP will learn that they cannot have everything the way they want it. They tell us we cannot put the postal workers back to work. We have had a very responsible debate started by the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke).
We have asked the government to bring in a free vote which I believe the people of Canada want to see, but the NDP oppose this. The premiers of their own party, including the premier of my province, put the meat people, the food people, and the wood people back to work. The premier of British Columbia must believe in the collective bargaining process because he has the support of labour. But he put them back to work because this was the responsible thing to do for British Columbia and Canada at this time. What this party is asking is that the postal workers be put back to work because this is what the people of Canada want, and it is what the majority of the postal workers want.
Some of the postal workers have spoken to me. I told the minister about one man who was harassed when he wanted
November 17, 1975

to go back to work. I hope the minister listens to us and not the diatribe coming from the members of the New Democratic Party.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I enter this debate tonight with some trepidation. It is after three o'clock in the morning.
Like most members of the House I am torn between the political expediency of a short-term solution as opposed to the long-term best interests of Canadians. I, perhaps among all members of this House will suffer more, as well as my constituents, as a result of the recent postal strike due to the fact that I have the largest mail order business in my riding. Five per cent of the industrial work force in my riding could be eliminated by this strike. My constituents, including those who possibly could lose their jobs because of this strike, are strongly in support of the stand taken by the Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey).
I think the Progressive Conservative party tonight has demonstrated real strength behind the Postmaster General, particularly in the motion moved by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), which asks for a free vote. What we want as parliamentarians is that they have a free vote.
I think the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) has shown irresponsible leadership in trying to have further confrontation. Perhaps he should read the speech of the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters), one of his colleagues, who probably gave the most intelligent speech given by any member of that party.
I think the Postmaster General is for labour. No one can deny his role as a spokesman for labour. I was amazed to hear the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) question the track record of the Postmaster General.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext: He is getting bored with the whole operation.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext:
I do not think so, I think he is showing leadership. I do not think 28 work stoppages in 20 months, 25 of them illegal, are an indication of leadership on the part of the union. These are the types of points that have been brought out tonight except by certain members from one particular party.
I do not think that forcing these people back to work is the solution to the problem. There is no question that we must develop some long-term solution. I think the Postmaster General has stood his ground and has not taken the easy way out. He has not recommended to this House or to the government that the workers should be forced back to work. I think that is real leadership. I am surprised tonight that with the track record of the Postmaster General, when for the first time he takes a very tough stand, all of a sudden everybody should attack him. I do not know anyone who more than the Postmaster General has stood his ground in very difficult times.
It is very late, Mr. Speaker. I have appreciated some of the comments that have been made tonight. I am sure consideration will be given to those who have made very conscientious and worthwhile contributions. The contribu-
Postal Strike
tions of others which have been critical, negative, and very irresponsible will show up on the record.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is now 3.11 a.m.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext:
I just wish first to thank the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke) for bringing the motion before the House this afternoon. It was a simple motion to the effect that this House do now adjourn.
It seems to me that all responsible members have taken the opportunity to bring before the Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey), who certainly is a very sensible person in this regard, their concern about what has been happening over the past 29 days.
I should also thank you, Mr. Speaker, for your gracious hospitality in seeing that members on both sides of the House were treated royally through the provision of sandwiches. We want to thank you for looking after us by giving us sustenance to carry on, and we thank my young colleague, the hon. member for Pembina (Mr. Elzinga), for seeing to it that hon. members received apples.
But most important we should give singular recognition to the staff who periodically become stuck in this sort of situation. Their devotion to duty is much appreciated and warmly received. We appreciate their steadiness, their reliability, and their understanding. This includes, of course, Hansard reporters and all of those who are still working in such magnificent form.
I can see that the press too is awake, God bless them. Usually at the end of a sitting around 10.30 p.m. or eleven o'clock there is only one member left in the press gallery. Now we have four. It shows you how important this debate is and how concerned they are about its result. Surely we all would dislike being here at this hour if nothing were to happen in the long run.
I say that collective bargaining is being questioned. With all our collective wisdom on both sides of the House and outside the House we have been talking about the collective bargaining process and the time honoured right to strike. We have been talking about the recent lock-out, and somebody spoke about the final offer, compulsory arbitration, and voluntary arbitration. We on this side submitted recommendations about implementing the proposal of the public disputes commission. We have heard about labour courts, and now we have the Finkelman investigation into the Public Service Staff Relations Act. I hope that this time they will look into the definition of essential services. This is something we have to be concerned about. The Canadian people are exercised over it; they want to know what the essential services are and what we should do to maintain them to protect the public interest.
I will not be much longer, Mr. Speaker, but I must chastise the minister, friendly as we may be. I think that this strike can be divided into two situations. One is the matter of public interest and the maintenance of essential service versus the collective bargaining process and all it stands for. Unquestionably sooner or later governments have to move in order to protect the public interest, and in

November 17, 1975
Postal Strike
our view the time has arrived to do so. The government says that in its judgment this is not the time.
Surely we all realize that some 17,000 letter carriers are losing something like $700,000, and that there are 22,000 inside workers losing $800,000 a day. We have this peculiar situation where 22,000 people govern the destiny of this country. This is what people are exercised about; they do not understand how it can happen in a democracy and how the government can be so insensitive to the needs of the public. The minister may say that people can use the courier services and telex. Let me tell him that these are restricted to only a few, but there are countless thousands of people who want the mail service to operate for any number of reasons. That is one situation.
The other situation-and I think the minister will respect me when I say this-is that the minister is out to break the union, particularly the executive. We all know that. We see an ego trip here. The Postmaster General is smiling because he knows I am right on; he is smiling like a Cheshire cat. He is on an ego trip. It is a declaration of war between the Postmaster General and Mr. Parrot and Mr. Davidson. Did you ever see such a confrontation in your life?
Usually the Postmaster General is a very smooth operator. This time he likes what he is doing, and I do not blame him, but what I do not like is that he is putting the whole load on the backs of the Canadian people. With all respect, that is shameful. Anyway, who will win in the long run? Because even if you break the back of the postal union you have not solved the problem. Apart from the union in Montreal we also know there is a radical movement in Toronto. Are they next? I am not throwing this out in the hope that it will happen, but we all know there is another problem in Toronto, the minister and I know it. He has tackled Montreal first, but is it fair, is it just that this battle take place on the backs of the Canadian people who rightly deserve the service for which they pay?
The minister has impeded the collective bargaining process as a result of the government's introduction of its policy under Bill C-73. I remember the shades of 1974. What is happening? As a result of the imposition of this
policy there can be a bargaining process at this time, but in any event it is a myth, because unlike the private sector those in the public sector can only go so far. If they think they have the bargaining process at hand they are mistaken. It is a myth, because when the public interest is adversely affected we have to step in and say, to heck with the collective bargaining process. This is being realistic and pragmatic.
I hope the minister will not carry on this battle with Davidson and Parrot much longer because he will not win and the unions will not win. I am also afraid that those who will really lose will be the Canadian people because the public interest cannot continue being affected so adversely. It is the minister's judgment. He was elected to lead. But surely the minister cannot be that insensitive to the needs of widows, of those who have families overseas, and to our overseas commitments and our trade.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext: What about casual workers?

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE STRIKE OF POSTAL WORKERS
speechtext:
Why don't you go to sleep as you have been all night, except for that last minute speech?
All I say is that we are looking for solutions. I do not have them. I put forward several alternatives. All sorts of things are happening in terms of what we can do to make the collective bargaining process work that much better.
The minister has the ball. It is up to him to catch it, carry it, and score a touchdown, as he has in the past. Let me say in conclusion; stop the theatrics with respect to your colleagues on the other side of the fence. The Canadian people appreciate what the minister has done but there comes a time when the public interest takes precedence, and in my view the time is now when provision of essential services is paramount.
